\chapter{Rank-one configurations near a point of a circle}
\label{chap:10-rank-one-configurations}

Results of the library's work on Diaz's conjecture, about the hypothesis that rank-one statements need. The six exponentials theorem (Chapter~\ref{chap:05-six-exponentials}) and Roy's strong six exponentials theorem \cite{Roy92} take as input a \emph{configuration}: $x_1,x_2$ linearly independent over $\Qbar$ and $y_1,y_2,y_3$ linearly independent over $\Qbar$, with all six products $x_iy_j$ in a given $\Qbar$-vector space. Near a point $u$ of a circle of algebraic radius, that is $u\neq0$ with $u\bar u$ algebraic, the chapter asks which spaces containing $H_0=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar\bar u$ carry one, and which of those Roy's theorem can use at a candidate. No statement here involves $e^{u}$, so all keep their content if Diaz's conjecture holds.

The first sections answer the question in small dimension. Generic data carry no configuration, whatever numbers are added (Theorem~\ref{thm:generic_circle_point_no_two_by_three_configuration}, called Theorem~A). The four-dimensional extensions $H_0+\Qbar z$ that carry one are exactly those containing $u^{2}$, $\bar u^{2}$ or some $1/(u-a)$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:circle_point_extension_two_by_three_configuration_iff}, called Theorem~B; several titles below use that name). In the power hulls $\Qbar u^{-k}+\Qbar u^{-1}+\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{k}$ a configuration exists only for $k=2$ and $k=3$, so through these hulls Roy's theorem excludes no single power beyond $u^{3}$ at a candidate (Theorem~\ref{thm:power_hull_strong_six_exp_configuration_iff}). The sections on separation and on Laurent hulls put these results into one mechanism over any field: separation (Theorem~\ref{thm:rank_one_config_separation}), the normal form of $2\times2$ configurations (Theorem~\ref{thm:circle_point_two_by_two_normal_form}) and configurations in Laurent hulls (Theorem~\ref{thm:laurent_hull_config_iff}).

The other sections are about five-dimensional spaces, where a configuration can escape the four-dimensional extensions. The section on five-dimensional extensions gives the first such spaces, $H_0+\Qbar z+\Qbar\bar z$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:circle_point_conjugate_pair_configuration_invisible_to_four_dimensional_extensions}). When the six products span only four dimensions (Case~I), the configuration is a geometric progression \cite[Lemma 4]{BSZ17}: two poles and every Möbius involution of the $u$-line give such spaces, and a progression whose ratio is rational in $u$ lies in a space that contains $u^{2}$, $u^{-2}$ or some $1/(u-b)$, or in an involution space (Theorem~\ref{thm:progression_space_contains_square_or_reciprocal_or_eq_involution_pencil_space}). When the products span the whole space (Case~II), the conjugation-stable spaces with a factor of degree one are the real pencil spaces (Theorem~\ref{thm:conj_equivariant_degree_one_space_eq_real_pencil_space}); the last section shows that a factor of degree two can occur without one of degree one (Theorems~\ref{thm:laurent_cubic_configuration_invisible_to_four_dimensional_extensions} and~\ref{thm:laurent_cubic_space_no_mobius_ratio_configuration}), that no factor of higher degree can (Theorem~\ref{thm:progression_pair_span_ratio_degree_le_two}), and which real pencil spaces with Laurent data the four-dimensional extensions see (Theorem~\ref{thm:laurent_real_pencil_configuration_invisible_to_four_dimensional_extensions} and Proposition~\ref{prop:laurent_real_pencil_space_contains_square_of_root}). The section on Case II beyond degree one ends with a formal member of each of the three families of conjugation-stable invisible spaces with a factor of degree two that the research notes classify, for every involution of the $u$-line that commutes with conjugation: two orbits fixed by conjugation (Proposition~\ref{prop:conj_stable_two_orbit_space}), two orbits exchanged by it (Theorem~\ref{thm:laurent_cubic_configuration_invisible_to_four_dimensional_extensions}, where they are $0$ and $\infty$, and Theorem~\ref{thm:conj_swapped_two_orbit_configuration_invisible_to_four_dimensional_extensions}), and a cyclic family (Theorem~\ref{thm:cyclic_pair_configuration_invisible_to_four_dimensional_extensions}). All the members use the involution $u\mapsto-u$, their configurations are those of \cite[Théorème 7(1)]{Dia07} at $v=u$, and the classification itself is not formalised. The section on polynomial hulls finds that $\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar\bar u+\Qbar P(u)+\Qbar\overline{P(u)}$ carries a configuration exactly when $\deg P\in\{2,3\}$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:polynomial_hull_two_by_three_configuration_iff}), real polynomials in $\operatorname{Re}u$ and $\operatorname{Im}u$ carry none (Corollary~\ref{cor:real_polynomial_hull_no_two_by_three_configuration}), and adjoining to $\widetilde{\mathcal L}$ a point of a circle that is transcendental over its field keeps Roy's theorem true (Theorem~\ref{thm:logAlgTilde_adjoin_circle_point_no_two_by_three_configuration}). The section on degree-one spaces says when Theorem~B sees a degree-one space $\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar\bar u+\Qbar g+\Qbar ug$, which always carries a configuration: exactly when $u\,R(u)\,g$ is a polynomial in $u$ of degree at most $3$ for some non-zero $R$ of degree at most $2$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:degree_one_space_visible_to_four_dimensional_extensions_iff_cubic_over_quadratic}). For rational data this is a bound on degrees, which decides every pencil space $W(\lambda,f)$ with rational $f$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:rational_pencil_space_visible_to_four_dimensional_extensions_iff_natDegree_le}). The section on polynomials in $u$ and $\bar u$ classifies the conjugation hulls of the polynomials $z$ in $u$ and $\bar u$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:laurent_conj_hull_two_by_three_configuration_iff}, called Theorem~E): $\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar\bar u+\Qbar z+\Qbar\bar z$ carries a configuration exactly when it is five-dimensional and in one of three disjoint classes, (P), (Q) and (R), and for exponents within $\pm3$ the criterion is explicit in the coefficients (Corollary~\ref{cor:cubic_window_conj_hull_two_by_three_configuration_iff_criterion}). The section on what the classical theorems cannot refute proves the rest of Theorem~D of the research note (Theorem~\ref{thm:logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_theorem_D}): at a point $u$ of a circle transcendental over the field of $\widetilde{\mathcal L}$, the space $\mathcal L+\Q u+\Q\bar u$ has the properties of Baker, Hermite–Lindemann, Gel'fond–Schneider, six and four exponentials and (relative to $\widetilde{\mathcal L}$) Roy, so these theorems, used as properties of $(\mathcal L,\widetilde{\mathcal L})$, cannot prove Diaz's conjecture (Corollary~\ref{cor:theorem_D_barrier}). The last section asks the question of Theorem~E for every $z$ rational in $u$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:rational_conj_hull_two_by_three_configuration_iff}, called Theorem~F): the conjugation hull $H_0+\Qbar z+\Qbar\bar z$ carries a configuration exactly when it is four-dimensional with $z\in H_0+\Qbar(u-a)^{-1}$ for some $a$ with $a\bar a=u\bar u$, or five-dimensional and of one of three types, given by a normal form for the configurations whose ratio $x_2/x_1$ is a rational function of $u$ of degree two (Theorem~\ref{thm:degree_two_configuration_normal_form}, called Theorem~NF). For $z$ a polynomial in $u$ and $\bar u$ with a five-dimensional hull, the hull has one of the three types exactly when it is in one of the classes of Theorem~E (Corollary~\ref{cor:laurent_conj_hull_configuration_shape_iff_class}); in the setting of Theorem~NF, the products $x_0y_j$ of a configuration with ratio $h=x_1/x_0$ span exactly the $f\in W$ with $hf\in W$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:degree_two_configuration_multiplier_space_eq}); and at a candidate, under Roy's theorem, Theorem~F's criterion excludes $z$ from $\widetilde{\mathcal L}$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:candidate_rational_conj_hull_criterion_not_mem_logAlgTilde}). Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources} says which of these results were not found in the sources read, and which are not routine.

\section{Generic data}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.generic_circle_point_no_two_by_three_configuration -- https://prove2.me/theorems/2f818ada-bb16-408c-9e9d-66186a87e8fb
\begin{theorem}[No configuration on generic data]
\label{thm:generic_circle_point_no_two_by_three_configuration}
\lean{Diaz.generic_circle_point_no_two_by_three_configuration}
\leanok
Let $u\neq0$ with $u\bar u$ algebraic, and let $w_1,\dots,w_m\in\C$ be such that $u,w_1,\dots,w_m$ are algebraically independent over $\Qbar$. Then there are no $x_1,x_2$, linearly independent over $\Qbar$, and $y_1,y_2,y_3$, linearly independent over $\Qbar$, with all six products $x_iy_j$ in $\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar\bar u+\sum_j\Qbar w_j$.

{\small\emph{Source:} Not found in the sources read; routine (Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources}). The case $m=0$ is \cite[Theorem 3.4]{Roy95} and \cite[Lemma 12.16 and Exercise 12.10]{Wal00}; see also \cite[\S3.2]{Roy95} and \cite[p.~186]{Fis01}. The general statement was not found in the sources read. It follows from Theorem~\ref{thm:rank_one_config_separation} and the bound $p+q\le4$ in the hull (Corollary~\ref{cor:generic_circle_point_config_is_two_by_two}).}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
Multiply by $u$. Since $\bar u=\rho/u$ with $\rho$ algebraic, every element of the space times $u$ is the value at $(u,w)$ of a polynomial over $\Qbar$ of total degree at most two that is constant once its first variable $X_0$ is set to $0$, and evaluation at $(u,w)$ is injective. A configuration therefore gives a rank-one $2\times3$ matrix of such polynomials, which factors as $(h,g)\otimes(c_0,c_1,c_2)$ with both factors free. Total degrees add, and $X_0\mapsto0$ is a ring map; each case puts two free vectors in a line or three in a plane.
\end{proof}

\section{Four-dimensional extensions}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.two_by_three_configuration_forces_progression -- https://prove2.me/theorems/46109c0d-3af4-46c3-900b-441e398cde5e
\begin{lemma}[A configuration in dimension four is a progression]
\label{lem:two_by_three_configuration_forces_progression}
\lean{Diaz.two_by_three_configuration_forces_progression}
\leanok
Let $V\subseteq\C$ be a $\Qbar$-vector subspace of dimension at most $4$, and let $x_1,x_2$ and $y_1,y_2,y_3$ be linearly independent over $\Qbar$ with all six products $x_iy_j$ in $V$. Then
\[ V=\Qbar\,b+\Qbar\,bh+\Qbar\,bh^{2}+\Qbar\,bh^{3} \]
for some $b\neq0$ and $h\notin\Qbar$.

{\small\emph{Source:} In print: \cite[Lemma 4]{BSZ17}, over any field. The converse direction, that such a progression carries a configuration, is used in \cite[Lemma 6.1]{Fis01} and \cite[Théorème 7(2)]{Dia07}.}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
Put $h=x_2/x_1$, which is not in $\Qbar$ and so is transcendental, and $B=x_1(\Qbar y_1+\Qbar y_2+\Qbar y_3)$. Both $B$ and $hB$ lie in $V$, so $W=B\cap hB$ has dimension at least $2$. The spaces $W$ and $h^{-1}W$ lie in $B$ and have dimension at least $2$, so they meet in some $c=hb\neq0$ with $b\in B$. Then $b,hb,h^{2}b\in B$ and $h^{3}b\in hB$: four free vectors in $V$.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.cubic_product_eq_square_normal_form -- https://prove2.me/theorems/bbd5da86-854b-4c2d-b59d-2fe6ec883487
\begin{lemma}[A normal form for $P_1P_2=P_0^2$]
\label{lem:cubic_product_eq_square_normal_form}
\lean{Diaz.cubic_product_eq_square_normal_form}
\leanok
Let $K$ be a field and $P_0,P_1,P_2\in K[X]$ with $\deg P_1,\deg P_2\le3$, $P_1P_2=P_0^{2}$, and $P_0,P_1$ linearly independent over $K$. Then there are $Q_0,Q_1\in K[X]$ of degree at most $1$, linearly independent over $K$, and $a,b\in K$ such that, with $g=aQ_0+bQ_1$,
\[ P_0=g\,Q_0Q_1,\qquad P_1=g\,Q_1^{2},\qquad P_2=g\,Q_0^{2}. \]

{\small\emph{Source:} Elementary.}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
Divide out a common factor: $P_0=dQ_0$ and $P_1=dQ_1$ with $Q_0,Q_1$ coprime. Then $Q_1P_2=dQ_0^{2}$, so $Q_1$ divides $d$, say $d=gQ_1$. Degrees add, so $\deg Q_i\le1$. A relation between $Q_0$ and $Q_1$ would be one between $P_0$ and $P_1$, so they are independent; one of them has degree $1$, hence $\deg g\le1$, and by Cramer's rule $g=aQ_0+bQ_1$.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.circle_hull_progression_contains_square_or_reciprocal -- https://prove2.me/theorems/1706d5e7-e333-42e4-8cad-2b8657fafca8
\begin{lemma}[A progression through $1$, $u$ and $\bar u$]
\label{lem:circle_hull_progression_contains_square_or_reciprocal}
\lean{Diaz.circle_hull_progression_contains_square_or_reciprocal}
\leanok
Let $u\in\C\setminus\Qbar$ with $u\bar u$ algebraic, let $b\neq0$ and $h\notin\Qbar$, and suppose that $V=\Qbar\,b+\Qbar\,bh+\Qbar\,bh^{2}+\Qbar\,bh^{3}$ contains $1$, $u$ and $\bar u$. Then $V$ contains $u^{2}$, or $\bar u^{2}$, or $1/(u-a)$ for some $a\in\Qbar$, $a\neq0$.

{\small\emph{Source:} A step of Theorem~\ref{thm:circle_point_extension_two_by_three_configuration_iff}.}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
\uses{lem:cubic_product_eq_square_normal_form}
Write $1=bP_0(h)$, $u=bP_1(h)$ and $u^{-1}=\bar u/(u\bar u)=bP_2(h)$ with $\deg P_i\le3$. As $h$ is transcendental, $P_1P_2=P_0^{2}$, and $P_0,P_1$ are independent because $u\notin\Qbar$. Lemma~\ref{lem:cubic_product_eq_square_normal_form} gives $g=aQ_0+cQ_1$ and $u=Q_1(h)/Q_0(h)$. If $c=0$, then $u^{2}=b\,aQ_1(h)^{3}$; if $a=0$, then $\bar u^{2}=b\,\rho^{2}c\,Q_0(h)^{3}$ with $\rho=u\bar u$; otherwise $1/(u+a/c)=b\,c\,Q_0(h)^{2}Q_1(h)$.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.circle_point_extension_carries_two_by_three_configuration -- https://prove2.me/theorems/dd39ce78-249e-4099-a7ff-76acfc50ff77
\begin{proposition}[Three spaces that carry a configuration]
\label{prop:circle_point_extension_carries_two_by_three_configuration}
\lean{Diaz.circle_point_extension_carries_two_by_three_configuration}
\leanok
Let $u\in\C\setminus\Qbar$ with $u\bar u$ algebraic, and let $w$ be $u^{2}$, $\bar u^{2}$, or $1/(u-a)$ with $a\in\Qbar$, $a\neq0$. Then there are $x_1,x_2$, linearly independent over $\Qbar$, and $y_1,y_2,y_3$, linearly independent over $\Qbar$, with all six products $x_iy_j$ in $\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar\bar u+\Qbar w$.

{\small\emph{Source:} The configurations behind \cite[Corollaire 5(1) and 5(4)]{Dia07}, used there with Roy's strong six exponentials theorem \cite{Roy92}.}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
Here $u^{-1}=\bar u/(u\bar u)$ lies in the space. Take $(1,u)\otimes(u^{-1},1,u)$ for $u^{2}$, $(1,u^{-1})\otimes(u,1,u^{-1})$ for $\bar u^{2}$, and $(u^{-1},(u-a)^{-1})\otimes(1,u,u^{2}-au)$ for $1/(u-a)$. The families are free because $u$ is transcendental; the last one uses $a\neq0$.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.circle_point_extension_two_by_three_configuration_iff -- https://prove2.me/theorems/f2c817ff-c9ef-49ae-94c0-78ef031172be
\begin{theorem}[The four-dimensional extensions that carry a configuration]
\label{thm:circle_point_extension_two_by_three_configuration_iff}
\lean{Diaz.circle_point_extension_two_by_three_configuration_iff}
\leanok
Let $u\in\C\setminus\Qbar$ with $u\bar u$ algebraic, put $H_0=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar\bar u$, and let $z\notin H_0$. There are $x_1,x_2$, linearly independent over $\Qbar$, and $y_1,y_2,y_3$, linearly independent over $\Qbar$, with all six products $x_iy_j$ in $H_0+\Qbar z$ if and only if $z\in H_0+\Qbar w$ for $w=u^{2}$, $w=\bar u^{2}$, or $w=1/(u-a)$ with $a\in\Qbar$, $a\neq0$.

{\small\emph{Source:} \textbf{Not found in the sources read, and not routine} (Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources}). With Roy's strong six exponentials theorem \cite{Roy92}, the ``if'' direction gives at a candidate the exclusions of \cite[Corollaire 5(1) and 5(4)]{Dia07}; every configuration has the shape of \cite[Lemma 6.1]{Fis01} and \cite[Théorème 7(2)]{Dia07}. Its key step, Lemma~\ref{lem:two_by_three_configuration_forces_progression}, is \cite[Lemma 4]{BSZ17}.}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
\uses{lem:two_by_three_configuration_forces_progression,lem:circle_hull_progression_contains_square_or_reciprocal,prop:circle_point_extension_carries_two_by_three_configuration}
If $z\in H_0+\Qbar w$ and $z\notin H_0$, then $H_0+\Qbar z=H_0+\Qbar w$, which carries a configuration by Proposition~\ref{prop:circle_point_extension_carries_two_by_three_configuration}. Conversely, Lemma~\ref{lem:two_by_three_configuration_forces_progression} writes $H_0+\Qbar z$ as $b(\Qbar+\Qbar h+\Qbar h^{2}+\Qbar h^{3})$ with $h\notin\Qbar$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:circle_hull_progression_contains_square_or_reciprocal} puts $u^{2}$, $\bar u^{2}$ or some $1/(u-a)$ in it. That element is not in $H_0$, since $u$ is transcendental, so $z\in H_0+\Qbar w$.

Since $\widetilde{\mathcal L}$, the $\Qbar$-span of $1$ and the logarithms of algebraic numbers, is closed under complex conjugation, a hypothesis $z\in\widetilde{\mathcal L}$ also brings $\bar z$; the five-dimensional spaces $H_0+\Qbar z+\Qbar\bar z$ are the subject of the next section.
\end{proof}

\section{Five-dimensional extensions}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.circle_point_conjugate_pair_extension_carries_two_by_three_configuration -- https://prove2.me/theorems/d8abac5b-9bd4-4091-a0ed-2be61713f899
\begin{proposition}[Two families of five-dimensional spaces that carry a configuration]
\label{prop:circle_point_conjugate_pair_extension_carries_two_by_three_configuration}
\lean{Diaz.circle_point_conjugate_pair_extension_carries_two_by_three_configuration}
\leanok
Let $u\in\C\setminus\Qbar$ with $\rho=u\bar u$ algebraic, let $a\in\Qbar$, $a\neq0$, and let $z=u/(u^{2}-a)$ if $a\bar a\neq\rho^{2}$, or $z=u/(u^{2}-a)^{2}$ if $a\bar a=\rho^{2}$. Then there are $x_1,x_2$, linearly independent over $\Qbar$, and $y_1,y_2,y_3$, linearly independent over $\Qbar$, with all six products $x_iy_j$ in $\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar\bar u+\Qbar z+\Qbar\bar z$.

{\small\emph{Source:} Rescaled, the configuration is the one in the proofs of \cite[Théorème 2]{Dia04} and \cite[Théorèmes 6(1) and 7(1)]{Dia07}, and the progression of \cite[Lemma 6.1]{Fis01}.}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
In the first case put $a'=\rho^{2}/\bar a$, which differs from $a$; then $\bar z=-(\rho/\bar a)\,u/(u^{2}-a')$, and let $b=1/(u(u^{2}-a)(u^{2}-a'))$. In the second, $\bar z=(\rho/\bar a^{2})\,u^{3}/(u^{2}-a)^{2}$, and let $b=1/(u(u^{2}-a)^{2})$. Partial fractions in $u^{2}$, with $u^{-1}=\bar u/\rho$, put $b,bu^{2},bu^{4},bu^{6}$ in the space, so $(1,u^{2})\otimes(b,bu^{2},bu^{4})$ is a configuration, free because $u$ is transcendental.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.circle_point_conjugate_pair_extension_excludes_squares_and_reciprocals -- https://prove2.me/theorems/f640cf63-2fec-48d4-b85e-1eff3f39da34
\begin{lemma}[What these spaces do not contain]
\label{lem:circle_point_conjugate_pair_extension_excludes_squares_and_reciprocals}
\lean{Diaz.circle_point_conjugate_pair_extension_excludes_squares_and_reciprocals}
\leanok
With $u$, $a$ and $z$ as in Proposition~\ref{prop:circle_point_conjugate_pair_extension_carries_two_by_three_configuration}, the space $\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar\bar u+\Qbar z+\Qbar\bar z$ contains neither $u^{2}$ nor $\bar u^{2}$, nor $1/(u-b)$ for any $b\in\Qbar$, $b\neq0$.

{\small\emph{Source:} Elementary.}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
Clearing denominators turns a membership into $A(u^{2})+u\,B(u^{2})=0$ with $A,B\in\Qbar[X]$. The same identity holds at $-u$, so $A=B=0$. For $u^{2}$ the odd part is not zero; for $\bar u^{2}=\rho^{2}/u^{2}$ the even part is not zero at $0$; for $1/(u-b)=(u+b)/(u^{2}-b^{2})$ the odd part is not zero at $b^{2}$.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.circle_point_conjugate_pair_configuration_invisible_to_four_dimensional_extensions -- https://prove2.me/theorems/901396cf-2688-4738-be1c-a80b6ff6e7c7
\begin{theorem}[Configurations invisible to the four-dimensional extensions]
\label{thm:circle_point_conjugate_pair_configuration_invisible_to_four_dimensional_extensions}
\lean{Diaz.circle_point_conjugate_pair_configuration_invisible_to_four_dimensional_extensions}
\leanok
With $u$, $a$ and $z$ as in Proposition~\ref{prop:circle_point_conjugate_pair_extension_carries_two_by_three_configuration}, put $H_0=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar\bar u$ and $W=H_0+\Qbar z+\Qbar\bar z$. Then $W$ carries a configuration, but for no $w\in W\setminus H_0$ does $H_0+\Qbar w$ carry one.

{\small\emph{Source:} Not found in the sources read, but routine (Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources}). The shape of the configuration is printed; see Proposition~\ref{prop:circle_point_conjugate_pair_extension_carries_two_by_three_configuration}.}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
\uses{prop:circle_point_conjugate_pair_extension_carries_two_by_three_configuration,lem:circle_point_conjugate_pair_extension_excludes_squares_and_reciprocals,thm:circle_point_extension_two_by_three_configuration_iff}
The configuration is Proposition~\ref{prop:circle_point_conjugate_pair_extension_carries_two_by_three_configuration}. If $H_0+\Qbar w$ carried one, Theorem~\ref{thm:circle_point_extension_two_by_three_configuration_iff} would give $w\in H_0+\Qbar t$ with $t$ one of $u^{2}$, $\bar u^{2}$, $1/(u-b)$. Since $w\notin H_0$, exchange puts $t$ in $H_0+\Qbar w\subseteq W$, against Lemma~\ref{lem:circle_point_conjugate_pair_extension_excludes_squares_and_reciprocals}. The configuration does not need all of $W$: its six products span the odd part $\Qbar u+\Qbar\bar u+\Qbar z+\Qbar\bar z$.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.conj_stable_circle_point_extension_no_two_by_three_configuration -- https://prove2.me/theorems/9819e926-24a6-4c12-8431-7a5f6be68dfa
\begin{proposition}[The conjugation-stable case carries none]
\label{prop:conj_stable_circle_point_extension_no_two_by_three_configuration}
\lean{Diaz.conj_stable_circle_point_extension_no_two_by_three_configuration}
\leanok
Let $u\in\C\setminus\Qbar$ with $\rho=u\bar u$ algebraic, and let $a\in\Qbar$, $a\neq0$, with $a\bar a=\rho^{2}$. Then there are no $x_1,x_2$, linearly independent over $\Qbar$, and $y_1,y_2,y_3$, linearly independent over $\Qbar$, with all six products $x_iy_j$ in $\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar\bar u+\Qbar\,u/(u^{2}-a)$.

{\small\emph{Source:} A consequence of Theorem~\ref{thm:circle_point_conjugate_pair_configuration_invisible_to_four_dimensional_extensions}. It is where the hypotheses of \cite[Théorème 2]{Dia04} and of \cite[Corollaire 4(4) and Théorème 7(1)]{Dia07} fail for this family.}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
\uses{thm:circle_point_conjugate_pair_configuration_invisible_to_four_dimensional_extensions}
Here $z=u/(u^{2}-a)$ has $\bar z=-(\rho/\bar a)z$, so the space is stable under conjugation. With $z_2=u/(u^{2}-a)^{2}$, the element $u/(u^{2}-a)=(\bar a^{2}/\rho)\bar z_2-az_2$ lies in $H_0+\Qbar z_2+\Qbar\bar z_2$ and not in $H_0$, so Theorem~\ref{thm:circle_point_conjugate_pair_configuration_invisible_to_four_dimensional_extensions} applies. When $a\bar a\neq\rho^{2}$, adding $\bar z$ gives a space that does carry a configuration.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.logAlg_conj_stable -- https://prove2.me/theorems/95246d4a-a61c-4120-bfd0-0f30ffec3055
\begin{lemma}[Conjugation keeps the logarithms]
\label{lem:logAlg_conj_stable}
\lean{Diaz.logAlg_conj_stable}
\leanok
If $\lambda$ is a logarithm of an algebraic number, so is $\bar\lambda$.

{\small\emph{Source:} Elementary.}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
$e^{\bar\lambda}=\overline{e^{\lambda}}$, and the conjugate of an algebraic number is algebraic.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.logAlgTilde_conj_stable -- https://prove2.me/theorems/9922f109-5be0-427a-93a2-e7015b8cdf9d
\begin{lemma}[Conjugation keeps $\widetilde{\mathcal L}$]
\label{lem:logAlgTilde_conj_stable}
\lean{Diaz.logAlgTilde_conj_stable}
\leanok
The $\Qbar$-vector space $\widetilde{\mathcal L}$ spanned by $1$ and the logarithms of algebraic numbers is closed under complex conjugation.

{\small\emph{Source:} Elementary; it is the stability that \cite[Théorème 2]{Dia04} uses.}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
\uses{lem:logAlg_conj_stable}
Conjugation fixes $1$, sends logarithms to logarithms (Lemma~\ref{lem:logAlg_conj_stable}), and $\overline{c\lambda}=\bar c\,\bar\lambda$ with $\bar c\in\Qbar$.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.candidate_div_sq_sub_not_mem_logAlgTilde -- https://prove2.me/theorems/35486890-e3f7-4a35-a512-441fc709f738
\begin{corollary}[Two exclusions at a candidate]
\label{cor:candidate_div_sq_sub_not_mem_logAlgTilde}
\lean{Diaz.candidate_div_sq_sub_not_mem_logAlgTilde}
\leanok
Assume Roy's strong six exponentials theorem, and let $u$ be a candidate: $u\neq0$, $|u|$ algebraic and $e^{u}$ algebraic. Let $a\in\Qbar$, $a\neq0$, and $\rho=u\bar u$. Then $u/(u^{2}-a)\notin\widetilde{\mathcal L}$ if $a\bar a\neq\rho^{2}$, and $u/(u^{2}-a)^{2}\notin\widetilde{\mathcal L}$ if $a\bar a=\rho^{2}$.

{\small\emph{Source:} One substitution in \cite[Théorème 2]{Dia04}, at $x=(u,\bar u)$ and $y=1/(u^{2}-a)$, and in \cite[Corollaire 4(4) and Théorème 7(1)]{Dia07}; the second part is \cite[Théorème 6(3)]{Dia07}. Roy's theorem is \cite{Roy92}.}
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
\uses{prop:circle_point_conjugate_pair_extension_carries_two_by_three_configuration,thm:hermite_lindemann_holds,lem:logAlg_conj_stable,lem:logAlgTilde_conj_stable}
$\widetilde{\mathcal L}$ is closed under conjugation and contains $1$, $u$ and $\bar u$, so $z\in\widetilde{\mathcal L}$ would put the space of Proposition~\ref{prop:circle_point_conjugate_pair_extension_carries_two_by_three_configuration} in $\widetilde{\mathcal L}$, with its configuration, against Roy's theorem.
\end{proof}

\section{Power hulls}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.power_hull_strong_six_exp_configuration_iff -- https://prove2.me/theorems/e31ad15c-0c6d-4572-b443-953da5c153e1
\begin{theorem}[Configurations in the power hulls]
\label{thm:power_hull_strong_six_exp_configuration_iff}
\lean{Diaz.power_hull_strong_six_exp_configuration_iff}
\leanok
Let $u\in\C\setminus\Qbar$ and $k\ge1$. There are $x_1,x_2$, linearly independent over $\Qbar$, and $y_1,y_2,y_3$, linearly independent over $\Qbar$, with all six products $x_iy_j$ in $\Qbar u^{-k}+\Qbar u^{-1}+\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{k}$ if and only if $k=2$ or $k=3$.

{\small\emph{Source:} Not found in the sources read; routine (Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources}). For $k=2,3$ the configurations are geometric progressions of four elements, which \cite[Théorème 7(2)]{Dia07} excludes from $\widetilde{\mathcal L}$ with Roy's theorem (\cite[Lemma 6.1]{Fis01} excludes them from $\mathcal L$ with the six exponentials theorem); at a candidate they give \cite[Corollaire 5(1) and 5(2)]{Dia07}. The direction ``only for $k=2,3$'' was not found; Diaz remarks that inside that theorem one cannot hope to go very far \cite[p.~390]{Dia07}. It is the case $S=\{0,\pm1,\pm k\}$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:laurent_hull_config_iff}; it concerns a single power $u^{k}$ through its hull, and Proposition~\ref{prop:power_pair_hull_two_by_three_iff} still excludes pairs of higher powers.}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
For $k=2$ take $(1,u)\otimes(u^{-1},1,u)$, and for $k=3$ take $(u,u^{-1})\otimes(1,u^{-2},u^{2})$. Conversely, multiply by $u^{k}$: the products become polynomials in $u$ supported on $\{0,k-1,k,k+1,2k\}$, and since $u$ is transcendental a rank-one $2\times3$ matrix of them, with free rows and columns, has rows that differ by a fixed non-zero shift of the orders at $0$. For $k=1$ and for $k\ge4$ no shift keeps three exponents of that set inside it.
\end{proof}

\section{Separation and the normal form}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.rank_one_config_separation_two -- https://prove2.me/theorems/fccd2c36-8b8a-4d53-b05f-e6d7a9c0803f
\begin{lemma}[Separation for one number]
\label{lem:rank_one_config_separation_two}
\lean{Diaz.rank_one_config_separation_two}
\leanok
Let $K\subseteq F$ be subfields of $\C$, $V_0\subseteq F$ a $K$-space and $w$ transcendental over $F$. If $x_1,x_2$ and $y_1,y_2$ are each linearly independent over $K$ and every $x_iy_j$ lies in $V_0+Kw$, then every $x_iy_j$ lies in $V_0$.

{\small\emph{Source:} Not found in the sources read; routine (Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources}).}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
Write $x_iy_j=c_{ij}+\ell_{ij}w$ with $c_{ij}\in V_0$, $\ell_{ij}\in K$. Since $w$ is transcendental over $F$ and $\det(C+wL)=0$, $\det L=0$. A non-zero column $j$ of $L$ gives $z=\ell_{2j}x_1-\ell_{1j}x_2\neq0$ with $zy_1,zy_2\in F$; comparing coefficients of $w$ in $(zy_1)(x_iy_2)=(zy_2)(x_iy_1)$ gives $z(\ell_{i2}y_1-\ell_{i1}y_2)=0$, so $L=0$ by the independence of $y$.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.rank_one_config_separation -- https://prove2.me/theorems/6412e225-68f7-4d31-b833-9e358b8177f0
\begin{theorem}[Separation]
\label{thm:rank_one_config_separation}
\lean{Diaz.rank_one_config_separation}
\leanok
A $p\times q$ \emph{configuration over $K$} in a $K$-space $V\subseteq\C$ is a pair of families $x_1,\dots,x_p$ and $y_1,\dots,y_q$, each linearly independent over $K$, with every product $x_iy_j$ in $V$.

Let $K\subseteq F$ be subfields of $\C$, $V_0\subseteq F$ a $K$-space and $w_1,\dots,w_m$ algebraically independent over $F$. Every $p\times q$ configuration over $K$ with $p,q\ge2$ in $V_0+Kw_1+\dots+Kw_m$ lies in $V_0$.

{\small\emph{Source:} Not found in the sources read; routine (Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources}). It contains the separation steps of Theorems~\ref{thm:generic_circle_point_no_two_by_three_configuration} and~\ref{thm:generic_period_never_enters}, which are over $\Qbar$. Its case $V_0=K=\Qbar$ follows from \cite[Proposition 12.2 and the Remark on p.~424]{Wal00}, whose argument it extends.}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
\uses{lem:rank_one_config_separation_two}
Induction on $m$, over $F(w_1,\dots,w_{m-1})$: every entry lies in a $2\times2$ block, to which Lemma~\ref{lem:rank_one_config_separation_two} applies.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.polynomial_submodule_trailing_degrees_card -- https://prove2.me/theorems/f604634b-5bd4-409c-ae3b-680a1e0bf0d4
\begin{lemma}[Orders at zero of a space of polynomials]
\label{lem:polynomial_submodule_trailing_degrees_card}
\lean{Diaz.polynomial_submodule_trailing_degrees_card}
\leanok
Let $K$ be a field and $X\subseteq K[X]$ a finite-dimensional $K$-space. The orders at $0$ of the non-zero elements of $X$ take exactly $\dim X$ values.

{\small\emph{Source:} Standard: the valuation argument of \cite[proof of Theorem 33]{BSZ17}.}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
Induction on $\dim X$: if $n_0$ is the least order, attained by $f_0$, the elements with coefficient $0$ at $X^{n_0}$ form a complement of $Kf_0$ whose orders are the others.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.polynomial_submodule_mul_finrank_ge -- https://prove2.me/theorems/493fa5ef-b99c-411b-8f1e-80c5901c9183
\begin{lemma}[Linear Cauchy--Davenport for polynomials]
\label{lem:polynomial_submodule_mul_finrank_ge}
\lean{Diaz.polynomial_submodule_mul_finrank_ge}
\leanok
For non-zero finite-dimensional $K$-spaces $X,Y\subseteq K[X]$, the span $XY$ of the products satisfies $\dim X+\dim Y\le\dim XY+1$.

{\small\emph{Source:} A case of the linear Cauchy--Davenport theorem of Eliahou and Lecouvey, as stated in \cite[Theorem 2]{BSZ17}.}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
\uses{lem:polynomial_submodule_trailing_degrees_card}
The order sets $A,B$ of $X,Y$ have $\dim X$ and $\dim Y$ elements (Lemma~\ref{lem:polynomial_submodule_trailing_degrees_card}), and $A+B$ lies in the order set of $XY$; Cauchy--Davenport in $\mathbb N$.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.rank_one_config_card_le_finrank_add_one -- https://prove2.me/theorems/13e9574b-ef87-4cc0-8354-7049fc6d19c6
\begin{proposition}[Configurations in a space of rational functions]
\label{prop:rank_one_config_card_le_finrank_add_one}
\lean{Diaz.rank_one_config_card_le_finrank_add_one}
\leanok
Let $u$ be transcendental over a subfield $K\subseteq\C$ and $V_0\subseteq K(u)$ a finite-dimensional $K$-space. Every $p\times q$ configuration over $K$ in $V_0$ has $p+q\le\dim V_0+1$.

{\small\emph{Source:} Not found in the sources read; routine (Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources}).}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
\uses{lem:polynomial_submodule_mul_finrank_ge}
Clear denominators: $g(u)x_iy_j=A_{ij}(u)$ with $A_{i1}A_{1j}=A_{11}A_{ij}$ in $K[X]$; the spans of the $A_{i1}$ and of the $A_{1j}$ have dimensions $p$ and $q$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:polynomial_submodule_mul_finrank_ge} bounds the span of their products, which embeds in $V_0$.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.circle_point_two_by_two_normal_form -- https://prove2.me/theorems/098df255-2e44-445e-a9ed-7b42a829b29d
\begin{theorem}[The normal form]
\label{thm:circle_point_two_by_two_normal_form}
\lean{Diaz.circle_point_two_by_two_normal_form}
\leanok
Let $u$ be transcendental over a subfield $K\subseteq\C$ with $\rho=u\bar u\in K$. Then $x_1,x_2$ and $y_1,y_2$ form a $2\times2$ configuration over $K$ in $K+Ku+K\bar u$ if and only if $x_i=\mu(P_{i1}+P_{i2}u)$ and $y_j=\mu^{-1}(Q_{1j}+Q_{2j}\bar u)$ for some $\mu\neq0$ and invertible $P,Q\in K^{2\times2}$: the configurations form the orbit of $(1,u)\otimes(1,\bar u)$ under $\mathrm{GL}_2(K)\times\mathrm{GL}_2(K)$.

{\small\emph{Source:} Not found in the sources read; routine (Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources}). It extends the two-dimensional critical-pair lemma of \cite[Lemmas 4 and 5]{BSZ17}; the configuration $(1,u)\otimes(1,\bar u)$ itself is \cite[p.~431]{Wal00}.}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
$ux_iy_j=A_{ij}(u)$ with $\deg A_{ij}\le2$, and the vanishing minor factors $A_{ij}=a_ib_j$ in $K[X]$ (extract a gcd). Neither the $a_i$ nor the $b_j$ are both constant, so all have degree at most $1$; then $x_i=\mu a_i(u)$ and $y_j=\mu^{-1}b_j(u)/u$, with $1/u=\bar u/\rho$.
\end{proof}

\end{corollary}

\leanok
\uses{cor:generic_circle_point_config_is_two_by_two,thm:circle_point_two_by_two_normal_form}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.two_by_two_config_critical_progression -- https://prove2.me/theorems/f27b3462-2ab3-4f63-9294-ba165ea51ef5
\begin{lemma}[Three products: a progression]
\label{lem:two_by_two_config_critical_progression}
\lean{Diaz.two_by_two_config_critical_progression}
\leanok
Let $x_1,x_2$ and $y_1,y_2$ be pairs, each linearly independent over a subfield $K\subseteq\C$, whose four products span a $K$-space of dimension $3$. Then $\operatorname{span}(x_1,x_2)=Ka+Kah$ and $\operatorname{span}(y_1,y_2)=Kb+Kbh$ for some $h\notin K$ and $a,b\neq0$.

{\small\emph{Source:} The dimension-2 case of \cite[Lemmas 4--5]{BSZ17}, stated there for a base field algebraically closed in the extension; here over any subfield.}

\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.two_sumset_iff_difference_count -- https://prove2.me/theorems/353f44e5-54a3-4e7c-928f-2a60c3e964ca
\begin{lemma}[Sumsets with two summands]
\label{lem:two_sumset_iff_difference_count}
\lean{Diaz.two_sumset_iff_difference_count}
\leanok
A finite $S\subseteq\Z$ contains $A+B$ with $|A|=2$, $|B|=q$ if and only if some $d>0$ has $\#\{s\in S:s+d\in S\}\ge q$.

{\small\emph{Source:} Elementary.}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
For $A=\{a,a+d\}$, $A+B\subseteq S$ says that $a+B$ lies in $\{s\in S:s+d\in S\}$.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.laurent_hull_config_iff -- https://prove2.me/theorems/183b9e0a-8947-48a2-bff4-40106fca6b4b
\begin{theorem}[Configurations in Laurent hulls]
\label{thm:laurent_hull_config_iff}
\lean{Diaz.laurent_hull_config_iff}
\leanok
A $p\times q$ \emph{configuration over $K$} in a $K$-space $V\subseteq\C$ is a pair of families $x_1,\dots,x_p$ and $y_1,\dots,y_q$, each linearly independent over $K$, with every product $x_iy_j$ in $V$.

Let $u$ be transcendental over a subfield $K\subseteq\C$ and $S\subseteq\Z$ finite. The $K$-span of the $u^s$, $s\in S$, carries a $p\times q$ configuration ($p,q\ge1$) if and only if $A+B\subseteq S$ for some $|A|=p$, $|B|=q$.

{\small\emph{Source:} Not found in the sources read; routine (Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources}). Theorem~\ref{thm:power_hull_strong_six_exp_configuration_iff} is the case $S=\{0,\pm1,\pm k\}$; the nearest printed result is \cite[Lemma 6.1]{Fis01}. Its proof is the valuation method of \cite[\S7]{BSZ17}.}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
\uses{lem:polynomial_submodule_trailing_degrees_card}
Distinct powers of $u$ are independent. Conversely, $P_{ij}(u)=u^Nx_iy_j$ with $P_{ij}$ supported on $S+N$; the spans of the $P_{i1}$ and the $P_{1j}$ have $p$ and $q$ orders at $0$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:polynomial_submodule_trailing_degrees_card}), and $fg=P_{11}h$ puts their sums, shifted, in $S$.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.power_pair_difference_count_iff -- https://prove2.me/theorems/c3c5d970-67d0-41e7-a528-b46b89849269
\begin{lemma}[Three equal differences in $\{0,\pm1,\pm k,\pm l\}$]
\label{lem:power_pair_difference_count_iff}
\lean{Diaz.power_pair_difference_count_iff}
\leanok
For integers $4\le k<l$, some difference occurs three times in $\{0,\pm1,\pm k,\pm l\}$ if and only if $l\in\{k+1,k+2,2k-1,2k,2k+1,3k\}$.

{\small\emph{Source:} Elementary.}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
The positive differences are $1,k-1,k,k+1,l-1,l,l+1,l-k,l+k$ twice each and $2,2k,2l$ once each; a third occurrence needs one of the six coincidences.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.power_pair_hull_two_by_three_iff -- https://prove2.me/theorems/41b0da9a-8258-4cd0-9035-a24bd38c09d3
\begin{proposition}[Pairs of powers]
\label{prop:power_pair_hull_two_by_three_iff}
\lean{Diaz.power_pair_hull_two_by_three_iff}
\leanok
Let $u$ be transcendental over a subfield $K\subseteq\C$ and $4\le k<l$. The span of the $u^s$, $s\in\{0,\pm1,\pm k,\pm l\}$, carries a $2\times3$ configuration if and only if $l\in\{k+1,k+2,2k-1,2k,2k+1,3k\}$.

{\small\emph{Source:} Not found in the sources read; routine (Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources}). The exclusions it gives at a candidate are substitutions in \cite{Dia07} (Corollary~\ref{cor:candidate_power_pair_not_both_mem_logAlgTilde}).}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
\uses{thm:laurent_hull_config_iff,lem:two_sumset_iff_difference_count,lem:power_pair_difference_count_iff}
Theorem~\ref{thm:laurent_hull_config_iff}, Lemma~\ref{lem:two_sumset_iff_difference_count} and Lemma~\ref{lem:power_pair_difference_count_iff}.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.four_pow_hull_no_two_by_three -- https://prove2.me/theorems/6c47ce09-6fa5-4025-90d3-ec6ef78e2208
\begin{proposition}[The powers $u^{4^j}$]
\label{prop:four_pow_hull_no_two_by_three}
\lean{Diaz.four_pow_hull_no_two_by_three}
\leanok
Let $u$ be transcendental over a subfield $K\subseteq\C$. The span of the $u^s$, $s\in\{0,\pm1\}\cup\{\pm4^j:j\ge1\}$, carries no $2\times3$ configuration. So at a candidate, Roy's theorem used through Laurent hulls cannot exclude $u^{4^j}\in\widetilde{\mathcal L}$ for all $j$.

{\small\emph{Source:} Not found in the sources read; routine (Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources}). Not in \cite{Dia07} (p.~390) nor \cite{Fis01}.}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
\uses{thm:laurent_hull_config_iff,lem:two_sumset_iff_difference_count}
Reduce to a finite part. For a pair $s<s+d$ with $M=\max(|s|,|s+d|)$, either $s=-M$, $d=2M$, or $|d-M|\le M/4$ and $s\in\{M-d,-M\}$; distinct non-zero absolute values differ by a factor at least $4$, so no difference occurs three times.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.candidate_power_pair_not_both_mem_logAlgTilde -- https://prove2.me/theorems/3706795a-5cd8-46fe-a412-48bb68de49e7
\begin{corollary}[Pairs of powers at a candidate]
\label{cor:candidate_power_pair_not_both_mem_logAlgTilde}
\lean{Diaz.candidate_power_pair_not_both_mem_logAlgTilde}
\leanok
Assume Roy's strong six exponentials theorem and let $u$ be a candidate. For $4\le k<l$ with $l\in\{k+1,k+2,2k-1,2k,2k+1,3k\}$, $u^k$ and $u^l$ are not both in $\widetilde{\mathcal L}$.

{\small\emph{Source:} Each case is one substitution in \cite{Dia07}: Corollaire 2(P)(1), Théorème 7(1), Corollaire 5(1)--(2), with $\bar u^{k}=\rho^{k}u^{-k}$.}
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
\uses{lem:logAlgTilde_conj_stable,thm:hermite_lindemann_holds}
By conjugation $u^s\in\widetilde{\mathcal L}$ for $s\in\{0,\pm1,\pm k,\pm l\}$; in each case an explicit $(u^a)_{a\in A}\otimes(u^b)_{b\in B}$ with $A+B\subseteq\{0,\pm1,\pm k,\pm l\}$ contradicts Roy's theorem.
\end{proof}

\section{Two poles}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.circle_point_two_pole_extension_carries_two_by_three_configuration -- https://prove2.me/theorems/9cdff91f-d194-421e-bd97-a3a72faf9979
\begin{proposition}[Two poles carry a configuration]
\label{prop:circle_point_two_pole_extension_carries_two_by_three_configuration}
\lean{Diaz.circle_point_two_pole_extension_carries_two_by_three_configuration}
\leanok
Let $u\in\C\setminus\Qbar$ with $\rho=u\bar u$ algebraic, $a_1\neq a_2$ non-zero algebraic numbers, $z_i=u/(u^{2}-a_i)$ and $W=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar\bar u+\Qbar z_1+\Qbar z_2$. Then $W$ carries a $2\times3$ configuration: $x=(1,u^{2})$, $y=(b,bu^{2},bu^{4})$ with $b=1/(u(u^{2}-a_1)(u^{2}-a_2))$.

{\small\emph{Source:} The progression of \cite[Lemma 6.1]{Fis01} and \cite[Théorème 7(2)]{Dia07}, with ratio $u^{2}$.}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
Partial fractions: $bu^{2}=(z_1-z_2)/(a_1-a_2)$, $bu^{4}=(a_1z_1-a_2z_2)/(a_1-a_2)$, $bu^{6}=u+(a_1^{2}z_1-a_2^{2}z_2)/(a_1-a_2)$, and $b$ is a combination of $u^{-1}=\bar u/\rho$, $z_1$, $z_2$.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.circle_point_two_pole_extension_excludes_squares_and_reciprocals -- https://prove2.me/theorems/2ea6a548-8444-48d0-9666-c224dac35020
\begin{lemma}[What two poles do not contain]
\label{lem:circle_point_two_pole_extension_excludes_squares_and_reciprocals}
\lean{Diaz.circle_point_two_pole_extension_excludes_squares_and_reciprocals}
\leanok
Let $u\in\C\setminus\Qbar$ with $\rho=u\bar u$ algebraic, $a_1\neq a_2$ non-zero algebraic numbers, $z_i=u/(u^{2}-a_i)$ and $W=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar\bar u+\Qbar z_1+\Qbar z_2$. Then $W$ contains none of $u^{2}$, $\bar u^{2}$ and $1/(u-c)$ with $c\in\Qbar$ non-zero.

{\small\emph{Source:} Elementary.}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
Every element of $W$ is a constant plus an odd function of $u$; clearing denominators gives $A(u^{2})+uB(u^{2})=0$, so $A=B=0$, and each of the three numbers has a non-zero part of the wrong parity.
\end{proof}

\section{Every involution}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.involution_pencil_space_carries_two_by_three_configuration -- https://prove2.me/theorems/b372d03d-7bb5-469f-93a0-efc25a44f423
\begin{proposition}[Every involution carries a configuration]
\label{prop:involution_pencil_space_carries_two_by_three_configuration}
\lean{Diaz.involution_pencil_space_carries_two_by_three_configuration}
\leanok
Let $u\in\C\setminus\Qbar$, let $q_1,q_2\in\Qbar[X]$ be coprime of degree at most $2$, one of degree exactly $2$ (so that $\Qbar q_1+\Qbar q_2$ is the pencil of quadratics vanishing on the orbits of a Möbius involution of the $u$-line), let $l_1,l_2$ be non-zero members of the pencil, and let $W$ be the span of $1,u,u^{-1}$ and of $q_1(u)^{i}q_2(u)^{3-i}/(u\,l_1(u)l_2(u))$, $i=0,\dots,3$. {\small\emph{Source:} The progression of \cite[Lemma 6.1]{Fis01}; that a critical configuration is a progression is \cite[Lemma 4]{BSZ17}.}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
$c=q_2(u)^{3}/(u\,l_1(u)l_2(u))$; $r$ is transcendental because $q_1,q_2$ are coprime.
\end{proof}

Let $K$ be a field and $a_0,a_1\in K[X]$ coprime with $1\leq\max(\deg a_0,\deg a_1)\leq2$. Then $Ka_0+Ka_1=Kp+Kq$ for a pair $(p,q)$ of one of the forms $(1,X)$; $(1,X^{2}+\alpha X)$ with $\alpha\in K$; $(X,X^{2}+\beta)$ with $\beta\neq0$; $(X+\beta,X^{2}+\gamma X)$ with $\beta\neq0$ and $\gamma\neq\beta$.

{\small\emph{Source:} Elementary; routine (Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources}).}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
Without $X^{2}$ terms the plane is $K+KX$. Otherwise it contains a monic $X^{2}+dX+e$ and a non-zero $r$ of degree at most $1$; $r$ constant, $r\in KX$ and $r\in K(X+\beta)$ with $\beta\neq0$ give the other three forms, the inequalities because $X$, resp. $X+\beta$, is not a common factor.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.laurent_window_factor_in_hull_plus_min_degree_line -- https://prove2.me/theorems/7238d170-e301-4e90-a1b3-29ab14185c30
\begin{lemma}[A degree count in a window]
\label{lem:laurent_window_factor_in_hull_plus_min_degree_line}
\lean{Diaz.laurent_window_factor_in_hull_plus_min_degree_line}
\leanok
Let $K$ be a field, $N\geq0$, $H_N=KX^{N-1}+KX^{N}+KX^{N+1}\subseteq K[X]$ (with $N-1$ read as $0$ when $N=0$), and $M\subseteq K[X]$ a subspace of dimension $2$ whose non-zero elements all have degree at least $N+2$. Then $M$ has a non-zero element $n$ of least degree such that, for all $p,q,y\in K[X]$ with $\deg p<\deg q$: if $py$ and $qy$ lie in $H_N+M$, then $py\in H_N+Kn$.

{\small\emph{Source:} Not found in the sources read; routine (Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources}). The degree count is in the manner of the valuation argument of \cite[\S7, proof of Theorem 33]{BSZ17}.}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
Write $py=h+m$ and $qy=h'+m'$ with $h,h'\in H_N$ and $m,m'\in M$. If $m\neq0$, then $\deg m=\deg py<\deg qy=\deg m'$, so $m,m'$ span $M$, and the minimality of $\deg n$ in $n=am+bm'$ forces $b=0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Two pencils with no three free factors]
\label{lem:laurent_window_quadratic_pencils_carry_no_three_factors}

\leanok
Let $K$ be a field, $N\geq0$, $H_N=KX^{N-1}+KX^{N}+KX^{N+1}\subseteq K[X]$, and $M\subseteq K[X]$ a subspace of dimension $2$ such that every non-zero $f\in M$ has $\ord f+2\leq N$ and $\deg f\geq N+2$, where $\ord f$ is the order of $f$ at $0$ (its trailing degree); call such an $M$ two-sided. Put $W=H_N+M$. There are no $\alpha\in K$ and free $b_0,b_1,b_2\in K[X]$ with $b_j\in W$ and $(X^{2}+\alpha X)b_j\in W$ for all $j$; and there are no $\beta,\gamma\in K$ with $\beta\neq0$ and free $b_0,b_1,b_2\in K[X]$ with $(X+\beta)b_j\in W$ and $(X^{2}+\gamma X)b_j\in W$ for all $j$.

{\small\emph{Source:} Not found in the sources read; routine (Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources}).}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
\uses{lem:laurent_window_factor_in_hull_plus_min_degree_line}

\end{proof}

\label{lem:laurent_conj_twisted_symmetric_normal_form}
\lean{Diaz.laurent_conj_twisted_symmetric_normal_form}
\leanok
Let $v\in\C\setminus\Qbar$ with $v\bar v=1$. Let $N\geq0$, $F\in\Qbar[X]$ and $g=F(v)/v^{N}$, and let $\gamma\in\Qbar$ with $\gamma\bar\gamma=1$ and $\bar g=\gamma vg$. Then there is $G\in\Qbar[X]$ with $G(0)=0$ and $g-\bigl(G(v)+\bar\gamma\,\overline{vG(v)}\bigr)\in\Qbar+\Qbar\bar v$.

{\small\emph{Source:} Not found in the sources read; routine (Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources}).}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
Divide $F=A+X^{N}B$ with $\deg A<N$ and put $G=B-B(0)$. As $\bar v=1/v$, $\overline{A(v)/v^{N}}$ is the value of a reflected polynomial, and comparing degrees in $\bar g=\gamma vg$, cleared at the transcendental $v$, gives $\overline{A(v)/v^{N}}=\gamma vG(v)+\gamma B(0)v$.

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.laurent_involution_space_carries_two_by_three_configuration -- https://prove2.me/theorems/b9e7a8bf-a58e-4cbc-ad2e-378af159d6c8
\begin{lemma}[The configuration of the involution spaces]
\label{lem:laurent_involution_space_carries_two_by_three_configuration}
\lean{Diaz.laurent_involution_space_carries_two_by_three_configuration}
\leanok

Then $1,v+\beta\bar v$ are free over $\Qbar$, so are $1,\bar v+e\beta v,\bar v^{2}+\zeta v+ev^{2}$, and the six products of a member of the first family with a member of the second lie in $S$. {\small\emph{Source:} In print: for $v=u/s$, $e\bar e=\beta\bar\beta=1$ and $\zeta=-\beta e^{2}\bar\zeta$, it is the configuration $x\otimes(1,y,\bar y)$ to which the proof of \cite[Théorème 2]{Dia04} applies the strong six exponentials theorem, at $x=(1,(u+\beta\bar u)/s)$; also \cite[Théorème 4(1)]{Dia07}. \leanok
Using only $v\bar v=1$, each product is an explicit combination of the generators, for instance $(v+\beta\bar v)(\bar v+e\beta v)=\beta(\bar v^{2}+ev^{2})+1+e\beta^{2}$; both families are free because a relation, cleared by $v$ or $v^{2}$, is a polynomial identity at the transcendental $v$.

\begin{proposition}[Conjugation-stable degree-one Laurent spaces]
\label{prop:laurent_degree_one_conj_stable_space_real_pencil_normal_form}
\lean{Diaz.laurent_degree_one_conj_stable_space_real_pencil_normal_form}
\leanok
Let $v\in\C\setminus\Qbar$ with $v\bar v=1$. Let $N\geq0$, $F\in\Qbar[X]$ and $g=F(v)/v^{N}$. Suppose $1,v,\bar v,g,vg$ are free over $\Qbar$ and $\bar g\in\Qbar+\Qbar v+\Qbar vg$, and let $W=\Qbar+\Qbar v+\Qbar\bar v+\Qbar g+\Qbar vg$. Then there are $\kappa\in\Qbar$ with $\kappa\bar\kappa=1$ and $G\in\Qbar[X]$ with $G(0)=0$ such that $\deg G\geq2$ or $v^{2}\in W$, and $W=\Qbar+\Qbar v+\Qbar\bar v+\Qbar h+\Qbar\bar h$ for $h=G(v)+\kappa\,\overline{vG(v)}$.

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.laurent_conj_hull_two_by_three_configuration_iff -- https://prove2.me/theorems/ca560c9f-536b-489e-a9c3-02cc24d09324
\begin{theorem}[Conjugation hulls of polynomials in $u$ and $\bar u$]
\label{thm:laurent_conj_hull_two_by_three_configuration_iff}
\lean{Diaz.laurent_conj_hull_two_by_three_configuration_iff}
\leanok
Let $u\in\C\setminus\Qbar$ and $s\in\Qbar$ with $s^{2}=u\bar u$ (so $s=\pm|u|$ is real), and put $v=u/s$, so that $\bar v=1/v$. Let $k\geq0$, let $c_j\in\Qbar$ for $j\in\Z$, and put $z=\sum_{j=-k}^{k}c_jv^{j}$ and $W=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar\bar u+\Qbar z+\Qbar\bar z$. Then $W$ carries a $2\times3$ configuration if and only if $\dim W=5$ and $W$ is in one of the following classes:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(P)] $\alpha u^{2}+\beta u^{3}\in W$ for some $\alpha,\beta\in\Qbar$, not both zero;
\item[(Q)] $W=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar\bar u+\Qbar(\bar v^{2}+ev^{2})+\Qbar(\beta\bar v^{3}+\zeta v^{2}+ev^{3})$ for some $e,\beta,\zeta\in\Qbar$ with $e\bar e=\beta\bar\beta=1$ and $\zeta=-\beta e^{2}\bar\zeta$;
\item[(R)] $W=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar\bar u+\Qbar g+\Qbar\bar g$ with $g=G(v)+\kappa\,\overline{vG(v)}$, for some $\kappa\in\Qbar$ with $\kappa\bar\kappa=1$ and some $G\in\Qbar[X]$ with $G(0)=0$ and $\deg G\geq2$.
\end{enumerate}
Since $u=sv$ and $\bar u=s\bar v$, the numbers $z$ are exactly the polynomials in $u$ and $\bar u$ with algebraic coefficients, $W$ is the conjugation hull of $z$, and $\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar\bar u=\Qbar+\Qbar v+\Qbar\bar v$. The three classes are pairwise disjoint (Proposition~\ref{prop:laurent_conj_hull_configuration_classes_disjoint}), and each forces $\dim W=5$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:laurent_conj_hull_class_finrank_eq_five}).

{\small\emph{Source:} \textbf{Not found in the sources read, and not routine} (Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources}). The ``only if'' half, the classification, was not found in the sources read; its method is partly that of \cite[\S7 and Lemma 4]{BSZ17}. The ``if'' half consists of printed configurations or substitutions in them: class (P) is \cite[Théorème 7(1)]{Dia07}, already in \cite[Théorème 2]{Dia04}; class (Q) is the configuration of the proof of \cite[Théorème 2]{Dia04} at $x=(1,(u+\beta\bar u)/s)$, also \cite[Théorème 4(1)]{Dia07}; class (R) consists of the real pencil spaces of Proposition~\ref{prop:conj_stable_real_pencil_space_carries_two_by_three_configuration}.}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
\uses{lem:laurent_involution_space_carries_two_by_three_configuration,lem:laurent_real_pencil_normal_form_carries_two_by_three_configuration,lem:laurent_conj_hull_with_polynomial_part_configuration_class,lem:laurent_conj_hull_finrank_le_four_no_two_by_three_configuration,prop:laurent_conj_hull_without_polynomial_part_configuration_classes,thm:polynomial_hull_two_by_three_configuration_iff}
With $v=u/s$ every space moves between $u$ and $v$. Only if: Lemma~\ref{lem:laurent_conj_hull_finrank_le_four_no_two_by_three_configuration} gives $\dim W=5$; then Lemma~\ref{lem:laurent_conj_hull_with_polynomial_part_configuration_class} gives (P) when $W$ contains a non-zero $v^{2}P(v)$, and Proposition~\ref{prop:laurent_conj_hull_without_polynomial_part_configuration_classes} gives (Q) or (R) otherwise. If: in class (P), $W$ contains the hull of $\alpha u^{2}+\beta u^{3}$, which carries a configuration by Theorem~\ref{thm:polynomial_hull_two_by_three_configuration_iff}; (Q) and (R) carry those of Lemmas~\ref{lem:laurent_involution_space_carries_two_by_three_configuration} and~\ref{lem:laurent_real_pencil_normal_form_carries_two_by_three_configuration}.
\end{proof}

\label{prop:laurent_conj_hull_configuration_classes_disjoint}

\leanok

\section{What the classical theorems cannot refute (Theorem D)}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.transcendental_add_mul_add_mul_conj -- https://prove2.me/theorems/6135a78a-d72e-4585-b66f-130ca72f4892
\begin{lemma}[Transcendence of $a+bu+c\bar u$]
\label{lem:transcendental_add_mul_add_mul_conj}
\lean{Diaz.transcendental_add_mul_add_mul_conj}
\leanok
Let $F$ be a subfield of $\C$ and $u\in\C$ transcendental over $F$ with $u\bar u\in F$. If $a,b,c\in F$ and $(b,c)\neq(0,0)$, then $a+bu+c\bar u$ is transcendental over $F$.

{\small\emph{Source:} Standard field theory.}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
With $e=a+bu+c\bar u$ and $\rho=u\bar u\neq0$, $u$ is a root of the non-zero polynomial $bX^{2}+(a-e)X+c\rho$ over $F(e)$; if $e$ were algebraic over $F$, so would be $u$.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.isAlgebraic_of_mem_of_isAlgebraic_adjoin_transcendental -- https://prove2.me/theorems/4f4c64ae-59ba-4efa-ae91-940fc9eda9b0
\begin{lemma}[Elements of $F$ algebraic over $\Q(w)$]
\label{lem:isAlgebraic_of_mem_of_isAlgebraic_adjoin_transcendental}
\lean{Diaz.isAlgebraic_of_mem_of_isAlgebraic_adjoin_transcendental}
\leanok
Let $F$ be a subfield of $\C$, $w\in\C$ transcendental over $F$, and $z\in F$ algebraic over $\Q(w)$. Then $z$ is algebraic.

{\small\emph{Source:} Standard field theory.}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
If $z$ were transcendental, $w$ would be transcendental over $\Q[z]\subseteq F$, so $(z,w)$ would be algebraically independent and $z$ transcendental over $\Q(w)$.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.isAlgebraic_of_hyperbola_pair_not_algebraicIndependent -- https://prove2.me/theorems/6c9029fe-9e52-42e8-a46b-108ff8056d72
\begin{lemma}[The hyperbola step]
\label{lem:isAlgebraic_of_hyperbola_pair_not_algebraicIndependent}
\lean{Diaz.isAlgebraic_of_hyperbola_pair_not_algebraicIndependent}
\leanok
Let $F$ be a subfield of $\C$, $u\in\C$ transcendental over $F$ with $u\bar u\in F$, and $c_1,c_2\in F$. If $c_1+u$ and $c_2+\bar u$ are algebraically dependent over $\Q$, then $c_1$ and $c_2$ are algebraic.

{\small\emph{Source:} Not found in the sources read; routine (Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources}).}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
\uses{lem:transcendental_add_mul_add_mul_conj,lem:isAlgebraic_adjoin_of_not_algebraicIndependent_pair}
$e_1=c_1+u$ is transcendental (Lemma~\ref{lem:transcendental_add_mul_add_mul_conj}), so $e_2=c_2+\bar u$ is algebraic over $\Q[e_1]$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:isAlgebraic_adjoin_of_not_algebraicIndependent_pair}): $\sum_{k\leq K}g_k(e_1)e_2^{k}=0$ with $g_K(e_1)\neq0$. As $c_2u+\rho=ue_2$, $\rho=u\bar u$, the polynomial $R(T)=\sum_kg_k(c_1+T)(c_2T+\rho)^{k}T^{K-k}$ over $F$ vanishes at $u$, so $R=0$ and $R(0)=g_K(c_1)\rho^{K}=0$; the same with $\bar u$ for $c_2$.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.mem_logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_iff -- https://prove2.me/theorems/fd55e4d6-c196-4201-a0a2-95fbe06faf50
\begin{lemma}[The space $\mathcal L_u$]
\label{lem:mem_logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_iff}
\lean{Diaz.mem_logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_iff}
\leanok
Let $\mathcal L$ be the set of logarithms of algebraic numbers, the $z\in\C$ with $e^{z}$ algebraic, and $\widetilde{\mathcal L}$ the $\Qbar$-span of $1$ and $\mathcal L$. Let $u\in\C$ and $\mathcal L_u=\operatorname{span}_{\Q}\mathcal L+\Q u+\Q\bar u$. Then $z\in\mathcal L_u$ if and only if $z=c+pu+q\bar u$ with $c\in\mathcal L$ and $p,q\in\Q$, and the $\Qbar$-span of $1$ and $\mathcal L_u$ is $\widetilde{\mathcal L}+\Qbar u+\Qbar\bar u$. At $u=0$ the membership criterion says that $\mathcal L$ is a $\Q$-vector space, so $\mathcal L_u=\mathcal L+\Q u+\Q\bar u$.

{\small\emph{Source:} Elementary.}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
\uses{lem:exp_ratMul_isAlgebraic}
$\mathcal L$ contains $0$ and is closed under addition, as $e^{a+b}=e^{a}e^{b}$, and under rational multiples (Lemma~\ref{lem:exp_ratMul_isAlgebraic}), so $\operatorname{span}_{\Q}\mathcal L=\mathcal L$; each $\Qbar$-span contains the generators of the other.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.exists_noncandidate_transcendental_on_circle -- https://prove2.me/theorems/d08bcf37-eb9f-4285-9ff0-4114280c0dce
% Statement written from the Lean source.
\begin{lemma}[A circle point off a countable field]
\label{lem:exists_noncandidate_transcendental_on_circle}
\lean{Diaz.exists_noncandidate_transcendental_on_circle}
\leanok
Let $K$ be a countable subfield of $\C$ and $\rho>0$ a real number. There is $t\in\C$ with $t\bar t=\rho$ that is transcendental over $K$ and has $e^{t}$ transcendental.

{\small\emph{Source:} Elementary: a countability argument.}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
The points $x+i\sqrt{\rho-x^{2}}$ with $|x|<\sqrt\rho$ form an uncountable set, while the numbers algebraic over $K$, and the $t$ with $e^{t}$ algebraic (countably many translates of $2\pi i\Z$), form countable sets.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.exists_circle_point_transcendental_over_logAlgTilde_closure -- https://prove2.me/theorems/2ca47967-6d09-4fc8-9af4-21a31e455b1f
\begin{lemma}[A circle point transcendental over the field of $\widetilde{\mathcal L}$]
\label{lem:exists_circle_point_transcendental_over_logAlgTilde_closure}
\lean{Diaz.exists_circle_point_transcendental_over_logAlgTilde_closure}
\leanok
Let $\mathcal L$ be the set of logarithms of algebraic numbers, the $z\in\C$ with $e^{z}$ algebraic, and $\widetilde{\mathcal L}$ the $\Qbar$-span of $1$ and $\mathcal L$. Let $F$ be the field generated by $\widetilde{\mathcal L}$ and $\rho>0$ a real number. Then $F$ is countable, and some $u\in\C$ with $u\bar u=\rho$ is transcendental over $F$.

{\small\emph{Source:} Elementary: a countability argument.}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
\uses{lem:exists_noncandidate_transcendental_on_circle}
$\mathcal L$ is a countable union of translates of $2\pi i\Z$, so $\widetilde{\mathcal L}$, spanned over the countable $\Qbar$, and the field it generates are countable; Lemma~\ref{lem:exists_noncandidate_transcendental_on_circle} with $K=F$.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_baker_number_field_basis -- https://prove2.me/theorems/664ef120-4687-4848-a81d-b89b2a11c8c8
\begin{proposition}[Baker's theorem over a number-field basis, for $\mathcal L_u$]
\label{prop:logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_baker_number_field_basis}
\lean{Diaz.logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_baker_number_field_basis}
\leanok
Let $\mathcal L$ be the set of logarithms of algebraic numbers, the $z\in\C$ with $e^{z}$ algebraic, and $\widetilde{\mathcal L}$ the $\Qbar$-span of $1$ and $\mathcal L$. Let $F$ be the field generated by $\widetilde{\mathcal L}$, let $u\in\C$ be transcendental over $F$ with $u\bar u$ algebraic, and put $\mathcal L_u=\mathcal L+\Q u+\Q\bar u$. Let $K\subseteq\C$ be a number field, $(\beta_k)$ a basis of $K$ over $\Q$, and $\ell_k\in\mathcal L_u$. If $\sum_k\beta_k\ell_k$ is algebraic, then $\ell_k=0$ for every $k$.

{\small\emph{Source:} Restates Baker's theorem \cite{Bak66} in the form of \cite[Theorem 4.5]{Wal00} (Theorem~\ref{thm:baker_number_field_basis}), with $\mathcal L$ replaced by $\mathcal L_u$; the $\mathcal L_u$ form was not found in the sources read; routine (Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources}).}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
\uses{lem:mem_logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_iff,lem:transcendental_add_mul_add_mul_conj,thm:baker_number_field_basis}
Write $\ell_k=c_k+p_ku+q_k\bar u$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:mem_logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_iff}); Lemma~\ref{lem:transcendental_add_mul_add_mul_conj} forces $\sum_k\beta_kp_k=\sum_k\beta_kq_k=0$, so every $p_k$ and $q_k$ is $0$, and Theorem~\ref{thm:baker_number_field_basis} applies to the $c_k\in\mathcal L$.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_baker_linear_forms -- https://prove2.me/theorems/910e0ef9-af0f-4fe0-a260-a0a4f7784b16
\begin{proposition}[Baker's theorem for $\mathcal L_u$]
\label{prop:logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_baker_linear_forms}
\lean{Diaz.logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_baker_linear_forms}
\leanok
Let $\mathcal L$ be the set of logarithms of algebraic numbers, the $z\in\C$ with $e^{z}$ algebraic, and $\widetilde{\mathcal L}$ the $\Qbar$-span of $1$ and $\mathcal L$. Let $F$ be the field generated by $\widetilde{\mathcal L}$, let $u\in\C$ be transcendental over $F$ with $u\bar u$ algebraic, and put $\mathcal L_u=\mathcal L+\Q u+\Q\bar u$. Let $l_1,\dots,l_n\in\mathcal L_u$ be linearly independent over $\Q$, and let $b_0,b_1,\dots,b_n$ be algebraic numbers, not all zero. Then $b_0+\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_il_i\neq0$.

{\small\emph{Source:} Restates Baker's theorem \cite{Bak66}, \cite[Theorem 1.6]{Wal00} (Theorem~\ref{thm:baker_linear_forms_in_logarithms}), with $\mathcal L$ replaced by $\mathcal L_u$, derived from the form of \cite[Theorem 4.5]{Wal00} as in \cite[\S4.2.5]{Wal00}; the $\mathcal L_u$ form was not found in the sources read; routine (Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources}).}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
\uses{prop:logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_baker_number_field_basis}
As in \cite[\S4.2.5]{Wal00}: write $b_j=\sum_ic_{ji}\beta_i$ in a $\Q$-basis $(\beta_i)$ of $\Q(b_1,\dots,b_n)$; Proposition~\ref{prop:logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_baker_number_field_basis} gives $\sum_jc_{ji}l_j=0$ for every $i$, so $c=0$, every $b_j=0$, and then $b_0=0$.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_hermite_lindemann_gelfond_schneider -- https://prove2.me/theorems/60ebe1e0-1afc-49a7-8e76-a9c865c50f8f
\begin{proposition}[Hermite–Lindemann and Gel'fond–Schneider for $\mathcal L_u$]
\label{prop:logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_hermite_lindemann_gelfond_schneider}
\lean{Diaz.logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_hermite_lindemann_gelfond_schneider}
\leanok
Let $\mathcal L$ be the set of logarithms of algebraic numbers, the $z\in\C$ with $e^{z}$ algebraic, and $\widetilde{\mathcal L}$ the $\Qbar$-span of $1$ and $\mathcal L$. Let $F$ be the field generated by $\widetilde{\mathcal L}$, let $u\in\C$ be transcendental over $F$ with $u\bar u$ algebraic, and put $\mathcal L_u=\mathcal L+\Q u+\Q\bar u$. Then $0$ is the only algebraic element of $\mathcal L_u$ (Hermite–Lindemann), and if $l_0\neq0$ and $\beta l_0$ lie in $\mathcal L_u$ with $\beta$ algebraic, then $\beta\in\Q$ (Gel'fond–Schneider).

{\small\emph{Source:} Restates the Hermite–Lindemann theorem \cite{Her1873,Lin1882} (Theorem~\ref{thm:hermite_lindemann_holds}) and the Gel'fond–Schneider theorem \cite{Gel34,Sch34} (Theorem~\ref{thm:gelfond_schneider}), with $\mathcal L$ replaced by $\mathcal L_u$, both derived from Baker's theorem for $\mathcal L_u$; the $\mathcal L_u$ form was not found in the sources read; routine (Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources}).}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
\uses{prop:logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_baker_linear_forms}
Proposition~\ref{prop:logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_baker_linear_forms} with $n=1$ and the form $-z+1\cdot z$; and with $n=2$, $b_0=0$ and the form $\beta\cdot l_0-1\cdot(\beta l_0)$, where $l_0$ and $\beta l_0$ are linearly independent over $\Q$ unless $\beta\in\Q$.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_six_exponentials -- https://prove2.me/theorems/98a6a8d9-0fa8-440b-a21d-2fbf37b69022
\begin{proposition}[The six exponentials theorem for $\mathcal L_u$]
\label{prop:logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_six_exponentials}
\lean{Diaz.logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_six_exponentials}
\leanok
Let $\mathcal L$ be the set of logarithms of algebraic numbers, the $z\in\C$ with $e^{z}$ algebraic, and $\widetilde{\mathcal L}$ the $\Qbar$-span of $1$ and $\mathcal L$. Let $F$ be the field generated by $\widetilde{\mathcal L}$, let $u\in\C$ be transcendental over $F$ with $u\bar u$ algebraic, and put $\mathcal L_u=\mathcal L+\Q u+\Q\bar u$. Then there are no $x_1,x_2$, linearly independent over $\Q$, and $y_1,y_2,y_3$, linearly independent over $\Q$, with all six products $x_iy_j$ in $\mathcal L_u$.

{\small\emph{Source:} Restates the six exponentials theorem \cite[Ch.~II]{Lang66}, \cite{Ram68}, \cite[Theorem 1.12]{Wal00} (Theorem~\ref{thm:six_exponentials}), with $\mathcal L$ replaced by $\mathcal L_u$; the dependent cases use Baker's theorem \cite{Bak66}. The $\mathcal L_u$ form, and a route to it that avoids Roy's strong six exponentials theorem \cite{Roy92}, were not found in the sources read; routine (Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources}).}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
\uses{lem:mem_logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_iff,lem:transcendental_add_mul_add_mul_conj,prop:logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_baker_linear_forms,prop:rank_one_config_inverse_adjoin,thm:six_exponentials}
Proposition~\ref{prop:logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_baker_linear_forms} makes both families linearly independent over $\Qbar$. As $\bar u=(u\bar u)u^{-1}$, Proposition~\ref{prop:rank_one_config_inverse_adjoin} with $K=\Qbar$ and $V_0=\widetilde{\mathcal L}$ puts the six products in $\widetilde{\mathcal L}\subseteq F$, Lemma~\ref{lem:transcendental_add_mul_add_mul_conj} then puts them in $\mathcal L$, and Theorem~\ref{thm:six_exponentials} applies. Roy's theorem is not used.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: Transcendence.quadratic_coeffs_eq_zero_of_transcendental -- https://prove2.me/theorems/0b946dc3-8d94-4797-b943-02e56589f23d
% Statement written from the Lean source.
\begin{lemma}[Quadratic relations at a transcendental number]
\label{lem:quadratic_coeffs_eq_zero_of_transcendental}
\lean{Transcendence.quadratic_coeffs_eq_zero_of_transcendental}
\leanok
Let $x\in\C$ be transcendental and $c_0,c_1,c_2$ algebraic with $c_2x^{2}+c_1x+c_0=0$. Then $c_0=c_1=c_2=0$.

{\small\emph{Source:} Elementary.}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
If $c_2\neq0$, $(2c_2x+c_1)^{2}=c_1^{2}-4c_2c_0$ makes $x$ algebraic; if $c_2=0\neq c_1$, so does $x=-c_0/c_1$; then $c_0=0$.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.det_zero_linear_forms_rank_one -- https://prove2.me/theorems/43368f52-e0aa-4270-9798-a38107dc9561
% Statement written from the Lean source.
\begin{lemma}[The lemma on linear forms over $\Q$]
\label{lem:det_zero_linear_forms_rank_one}
\lean{Diaz.det_zero_linear_forms_rank_one}
\leanok
Let $M=(L_{ij})_{i,j=1,2}$ be a matrix of linear forms $L_{ij}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}a_{ijk}X_k$ with $a_{ijk}\in\Q$. If $L_{11}L_{22}=L_{12}L_{21}$, that is $a_{11k}a_{22l}+a_{11l}a_{22k}=a_{12k}a_{21l}+a_{12l}a_{21k}$ for all $k,l$, then the rows of $M$ are linearly dependent over $\Q$, or its columns are.

{\small\emph{Source:} Elementary; it is the case $F=\Q$ of Lemma~\ref{lem:det_zero_linear_forms_rank_one_field}.}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
If $L_{11}=0$, then $L_{12}L_{21}=0$, a zero row or a zero column. Otherwise, with $\alpha=a_{11k}\neq0$, $(\alpha L_{12}-a_{12k}L_{11})(\alpha L_{21}-a_{21k}L_{11})=0$, and then $\alpha L_{22}=a_{12k}L_{21}$ (the columns are proportional) or $\alpha L_{22}=a_{21k}L_{12}$ (the rows are).
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.four_exp_barrier_of_no_quadratic_relation -- https://prove2.me/theorems/ff0f40a7-c2f2-44ce-803f-5f76aefbeae5
% Statement written from the Lean source.
\begin{lemma}[Singular matrices without a quadratic relation]
\label{lem:four_exp_barrier_of_no_quadratic_relation}
\lean{Diaz.four_exp_barrier_of_no_quadratic_relation}
\leanok
Let $e_1,\dots,e_n\in\C$ satisfy no quadratic relation over $\Q$: if $\sum_{k,l}f_{kl}e_ke_l=0$ with $f_{kl}\in\Q$, then $f_{kl}+f_{lk}=0$ for all $k,l$. Let $M=(m_{ij})_{i,j=1,2}$ with $m_{ij}=\sum_ka_{ijk}e_k$ and $a_{ijk}\in\Q$. If $\det M=0$, then the rows of $M$ are linearly dependent over $\Q$, or its columns are.

{\small\emph{Source:} Elementary.}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
\uses{lem:det_zero_linear_forms_rank_one}
$\det M=\sum_{k,l}(a_{11k}a_{22l}-a_{12k}a_{21l})e_ke_l$, so the forms $L_{ij}=\sum_ka_{ijk}X_k$ satisfy $L_{11}L_{22}=L_{12}L_{21}$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:det_zero_linear_forms_rank_one} gives a rational relation between their rows or columns, which holds at $e$.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_four_exponentials_trdeg_one -- https://prove2.me/theorems/3c7780b0-825d-4d08-89b1-fe91d68b1e3f
\begin{proposition}[Four exponentials in transcendence degree one, for $\mathcal L_u$]
\label{prop:logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_four_exponentials_trdeg_one}
\lean{Diaz.logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_four_exponentials_trdeg_one}
\leanok
Let $\mathcal L$ be the set of logarithms of algebraic numbers, the $z\in\C$ with $e^{z}$ algebraic, and $\widetilde{\mathcal L}$ the $\Qbar$-span of $1$ and $\mathcal L$. Let $F$ be the field generated by $\widetilde{\mathcal L}$, let $u\in\C$ be transcendental over $F$ with $u\bar u$ algebraic, and put $\mathcal L_u=\mathcal L+\Q u+\Q\bar u$. Let $\ell_{11},\ell_{12},\ell_{21},\ell_{22}\in\mathcal L_u$ be non-zero with $\ell_{11}\ell_{22}=\ell_{12}\ell_{21}$ and $\trdeg_{\Q}\Q[\ell_{11},\ell_{12},\ell_{21},\ell_{22}]\leq1$. Then the two rows, or the two columns, of $\begin{pmatrix}\ell_{11}&\ell_{12}\\\ell_{21}&\ell_{22}\end{pmatrix}$ are linearly dependent over $\Q$.

{\small\emph{Source:} Restates the four exponentials theorem in transcendence degree one \cite[Cor.~4]{W73}, \cite[Cor.~7]{Bro74} (Theorem~\ref{thm:four_exponentials_trdeg_one}), with $\mathcal L$ replaced by $\mathcal L_u$; the $\mathcal L_u$ form was not found in the sources read; routine (Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources}).}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
\uses{lem:logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_trdeg_le_one_trichotomy,thm:four_exponentials_trdeg_one,lem:four_exp_barrier_of_no_quadratic_relation,lem:quadratic_coeffs_eq_zero_of_transcendental}
Lemma~\ref{lem:logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_trdeg_le_one_trichotomy}: entries in $\mathcal L$ are Theorem~\ref{thm:four_exponentials_trdeg_one}; entries on a line $\Q e$ give proportional rows; entries in $\Q u+\Q\bar u$ are Lemma~\ref{lem:four_exp_barrier_of_no_quadratic_relation} at $(u,\bar u)$, since $au^{2}+bu\bar u+c\bar u^{2}=0$, times $u^{2}$, is a quadratic relation with algebraic coefficients for the transcendental $u^{2}$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:quadratic_coeffs_eq_zero_of_transcendental}).
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_theorem_D -- https://prove2.me/theorems/a03faab5-0e0d-4f60-899e-26416e5379d4
\begin{theorem}[Theorem D: the classical theorems for $\mathcal L_u$]
\label{thm:logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_theorem_D}
\lean{Diaz.logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_theorem_D}
\leanok
Let $\mathcal L$ be the set of logarithms of algebraic numbers, the $z\in\C$ with $e^{z}$ algebraic, and $\widetilde{\mathcal L}$ the $\Qbar$-span of $1$ and $\mathcal L$. Let $F$ be the field generated by $\widetilde{\mathcal L}$, let $u\in\C$ be transcendental over $F$ with $u\bar u$ algebraic, and put $\mathcal L_u=\mathcal L+\Q u+\Q\bar u$. Say that a $\Q$-vector subspace $L\subseteq\C$ has the \emph{Theorem~D properties} if, with $\widetilde L$ the $\Qbar$-span of $1$ and $L$:
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{conjugation:} $\bar z\in L$ for every $z\in L$;
\item \emph{Baker:} if $l_1,\dots,l_n\in L$ are linearly independent over $\Q$ and $b_0,b_1,\dots,b_n$ are algebraic, not all zero, then $b_0+\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_il_i\neq0$;
\item \emph{Hermite–Lindemann:} $0$ is the only algebraic element of $L$;
\item \emph{Gel'fond–Schneider:} if $l_0\neq0$ and $\beta l_0$ lie in $L$ and $\beta$ is algebraic, then $\beta\in\Q$;
\item \emph{Roy, relative to $\widetilde{\mathcal L}$:} if there is no $2\times3$ configuration in $\widetilde{\mathcal L}$, there is none in $\widetilde L$;
\item \emph{six exponentials:} there are no $x_1,x_2$, linearly independent over $\Q$, and $y_1,y_2,y_3$, linearly independent over $\Q$, with all six products $x_iy_j$ in $L$;
\item \emph{four exponentials in transcendence degree one:} if $\ell_{11},\ell_{12},\ell_{21},\ell_{22}\in L$ are non-zero, $\ell_{11}\ell_{22}=\ell_{12}\ell_{21}$ and $\trdeg_{\Q}\Q[\ell_{11},\ell_{12},\ell_{21},\ell_{22}]\leq1$, then the rows, or the columns, of $(\ell_{ij})$ are linearly dependent over $\Q$.
\end{itemize}
Then $\mathcal L\subseteq\mathcal L_u$, $u\in\mathcal L_u$, $u\notin\Qbar$, $u\neq0$ and $|u|$ is algebraic, and $\mathcal L_u$ has the Theorem~D properties; for it, $\widetilde L=\widetilde{\mathcal L}+\Qbar u+\Qbar\bar u$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:mem_logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_iff}). The Roy clause is an implication, so the statement is unconditional, and $e^{u}$ is not involved.

{\small\emph{Source:} Not found in the sources read; routine (Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources}). With $\mathcal L$ replaced by $\mathcal L_u$, each clause restates a classical theorem: Baker \cite{Bak66}, Hermite–Lindemann \cite{Her1873,Lin1882}, Gel'fond–Schneider \cite{Gel34,Sch34}, six exponentials \cite[Ch.~II]{Lang66}, \cite{Ram68}, four exponentials in transcendence degree one \cite[Cor.~4]{W73}, \cite[Cor.~7]{Bro74}, and, as an implication, Roy's strong six exponentials theorem \cite[Corollary 2]{Roy92}.}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
\uses{lem:mem_logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_iff,prop:logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_baker_linear_forms,prop:logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_hermite_lindemann_gelfond_schneider,prop:logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_six_exponentials,prop:logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_four_exponentials_trdeg_one,thm:logAlgTilde_adjoin_circle_point_no_two_by_three_configuration,lem:logAlg_conj_stable}
$u\notin\Qbar$ as $\Qbar\subseteq F$, and $|u|^{2}=u\bar u$. Conjugation by Lemmas~\ref{lem:mem_logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_iff} and~\ref{lem:logAlg_conj_stable}; Baker, Hermite–Lindemann and Gel'fond–Schneider are Propositions~\ref{prop:logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_baker_linear_forms} and~\ref{prop:logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_hermite_lindemann_gelfond_schneider}, six and four exponentials Propositions~\ref{prop:logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_six_exponentials} and~\ref{prop:logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_four_exponentials_trdeg_one}; Roy is Theorem~\ref{thm:logAlgTilde_adjoin_circle_point_no_two_by_three_configuration}, as $\widetilde L=\widetilde{\mathcal L}+\Qbar u+\Qbar\bar u$.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.span_logAlg_theorem_D_properties -- https://prove2.me/theorems/3c674580-9a0c-42dd-b958-1221cd425017
\begin{proposition}[The Theorem D properties of $\mathcal L$]
\label{prop:span_logAlg_theorem_D_properties}
\lean{Diaz.span_logAlg_theorem_D_properties}
\leanok
Let $\mathcal L$ be the set of logarithms of algebraic numbers, the $z\in\C$ with $e^{z}$ algebraic, and $\widetilde{\mathcal L}$ the $\Qbar$-span of $1$ and $\mathcal L$. Let $L=\operatorname{span}_{\Q}\mathcal L$, which is $\mathcal L$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:mem_logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_iff}). Then Diaz's conjecture, that $e^{u}$ is transcendental for every $u\neq0$ with $|u|$ algebraic, holds if and only if no non-zero $u\in L$ has $|u|$ algebraic; and $L$ has the Theorem~D properties of Theorem~\ref{thm:logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_theorem_D}, with $\widetilde L=\widetilde{\mathcal L}$.

{\small\emph{Source:} Not found in the sources read as a bundle; routine (Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources}). The clauses are classical theorems about $\mathcal L$: Baker \cite{Bak66}, Hermite–Lindemann \cite{Her1873,Lin1882}, Gel'fond–Schneider \cite{Gel34,Sch34}, six exponentials \cite[Ch.~II]{Lang66}, \cite{Ram68} and four exponentials in transcendence degree one \cite[Cor.~4]{W73}, \cite[Cor.~7]{Bro74}; the Roy clause is relative, so Roy's theorem \cite[Corollary 2]{Roy92} is not needed.}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
\uses{lem:mem_logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_iff,thm:baker_linear_forms_in_logarithms,thm:hermite_lindemann_holds,thm:gelfond_schneider,thm:six_exponentials,thm:four_exponentials_trdeg_one,lem:logAlg_conj_stable}
$L=\mathcal L$, so Diaz's conjecture is the contrapositive. The clauses are Lemma~\ref{lem:logAlg_conj_stable} and Theorems~\ref{thm:baker_linear_forms_in_logarithms}, \ref{thm:hermite_lindemann_holds}, \ref{thm:gelfond_schneider} (a non-rational $\beta$ would make $e^{\beta l_0}$ transcendental), \ref{thm:six_exponentials} and~\ref{thm:four_exponentials_trdeg_one}; the Roy clause holds as $\widetilde L=\widetilde{\mathcal L}$.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.theorem_D_barrier -- https://prove2.me/theorems/6139da34-dd78-4fe4-8944-db9c355225ca
\begin{corollary}[Theorem D as a barrier]
\label{cor:theorem_D_barrier}
\lean{Diaz.theorem_D_barrier}
\leanok
Let $\mathcal L$ be the set of logarithms of algebraic numbers, the $z\in\C$ with $e^{z}$ algebraic, and $\widetilde{\mathcal L}$ the $\Qbar$-span of $1$ and $\mathcal L$. There is a $\Q$-vector subspace $L\subseteq\C$ with $\mathcal L\subseteq L$ that has the Theorem~D properties of Theorem~\ref{thm:logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_theorem_D} and contains some $u\neq0$ with $|u|$ algebraic. So these properties, as properties of $(\mathcal L,\widetilde{\mathcal L})$, with Roy's theorem for $\widetilde{\mathcal L}$ \cite[Corollary 2]{Roy92} supplying the hypothesis of the Roy clause, do not prove Diaz's conjecture: by Proposition~\ref{prop:span_logAlg_theorem_D_properties} the conjecture says that no such $u$ lies in $\mathcal L$, and an argument from the properties alone would apply to $L$ as well.
