Lemma~\ref{lem:exists_circle_point_transcendental_over_logAlgTilde_closure} at $\rho=1$ gives $u$ with $u\bar u=1$, transcendental over the field generated by $\widetilde{\mathcal L}$; Theorem~\ref{thm:logAlg_adjoin_circle_point_theorem_D} for $L=\mathcal L_u$.
\end{proof}

\section{Rational hulls: the degree-two normal form and Theorem F}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.quadratic_pencil_wronskian_identities -- https://prove2.me/theorems/6336441d-f72e-4c21-b1dc-e6c693613e46
\begin{lemma}[The Wronskian of a quadratic pencil]
\label{lem:quadratic_pencil_wronskian_identities}
\lean{Diaz.quadratic_pencil_wronskian_identities}
\leanok
Let $K$ be a commutative ring and $p,q\in K[X]$ of degree at most $2$, with coefficients $p_i,q_i$ of $X^{i}$, and let $J=p'q-pq'$ be their Wronskian. Then $J=(p_2q_1-p_1q_2)X^{2}+2(p_2q_0-p_0q_2)X+(p_1q_0-p_0q_1)$ and $J^{2}=d_2p^{2}+d_1pq+d_0q^{2}$, with $d_2=q_1^{2}-4q_2q_0$, $d_1=4(p_2q_0+p_0q_2)-2p_1q_1$ and $d_0=p_1^{2}-4p_2p_0$. Here $d_2X^{2}+d_1X+d_0$ is the discriminant, in $Y$, of $p(Y)-Xq(Y)$; with $[ij]=p_iq_j-p_jq_i$, the first identity reads $J=[21]X^{2}+2[20]X+[10]$.

{\small\emph{Source:} Classical: the Wronskian of a pencil of binary quadratics, whose square is the discriminant of the pencil written as a quadratic form in its two members.}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
Both identities are polynomial identities in the six coefficients: expand $p$ and $q$, differentiate term by term, and normalise in the commutative ring $K$.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.quadratic_pencil_resultant_ne_zero -- https://prove2.me/theorems/71979ac5-d1c9-4fad-8dc4-65c8e2670d78
\begin{lemma}[The resultant of a coprime quadratic pencil]
\label{lem:quadratic_pencil_resultant_ne_zero}
\lean{Diaz.quadratic_pencil_resultant_ne_zero}
\leanok
Let $K$ be a field of characteristic zero and $p,q\in K[X]$ coprime with $\max(\deg p,\deg q)=2$; write $p_i,q_i$ for the coefficients of $X^{i}$ and $[ij]=p_iq_j-p_jq_i$. Then $\Res=[20]^{2}-[21][10]\neq0$. Up to sign, $\Res$ is the determinant of the Bezout matrix of $p$ and $q$, their resultant as binary quadratic forms.

{\small\emph{Source:} Classical: the resultant of two binary quadratics, up to sign the determinant of their Bezout matrix, vanishes only when they have a common factor.}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
\uses{lem:quadratic_pencil_wronskian_identities}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:quadratic_pencil_wronskian_identities} the coefficient matrix of $(q,p,J)$ in $(1,X,X^{2})$ has determinant $-2\Res$. If $\Res=0$, some $v\neq0$ has $v_0q+v_1p+v_2J=0$: $v_2=0$ makes $p,q$ proportional, so both constant by coprimality; $v_2\neq0$ gives $(v_2p'+v_0)q=p(v_2q'-v_1)$, so the one of $p,q$ of degree $2$ divides a polynomial of degree at most $1$ whose coefficient of $X$ is $2v_2$ times its leading coefficient, non-zero in characteristic zero.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.quadratic_pencil_wronskian_span -- https://prove2.me/theorems/b117f552-73c4-49b8-9c3b-beb302620a80
\begin{lemma}[A coprime quadratic pencil and its Wronskian span the quadratics]
\label{lem:quadratic_pencil_wronskian_span}
\lean{Diaz.quadratic_pencil_wronskian_span}
\leanok
Let $K$ be a field of characteristic zero, $p,q\in K[X]$ coprime with $\max(\deg p,\deg q)=2$, and $J=p'q-pq'$. Then every $R\in K[X]$ of degree at most $2$ is $aq+bp+cJ$ for some $a,b,c\in K$. Characteristic zero is needed: in characteristic $2$, $p=X^{2}$ and $q=1$ give $J=0$.

{\small\emph{Source:} Classical: two binary quadratics with non-zero resultant and their Wronskian span the binary quadratics.}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
\uses{lem:quadratic_pencil_wronskian_identities,lem:quadratic_pencil_resultant_ne_zero}
In the basis $1$, $X$, $X^{2}$, the coefficient matrix $M$ of $q$, $p$ and $J$ has determinant $-2\Res$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:quadratic_pencil_wronskian_identities}), which is non-zero by Lemma~\ref{lem:quadratic_pencil_resultant_ne_zero}; for $r$ the coefficient vector of $R$, $v=rM^{-1}$ gives $R=v_0q+v_1p+v_2J$.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.coprime_pencil_mobius -- https://prove2.me/theorems/b442a6ed-6d2d-437a-aeaf-a697bfa9a130
\begin{lemma}[A change of basis of a coprime quadratic pencil]
\label{lem:coprime_pencil_mobius}
\lean{Diaz.coprime_pencil_mobius}
\leanok
Let $K$ be a field, $p,q\in K[X]$ coprime with $\max(\deg p,\deg q)=2$, and $a,b,c,d\in K$ with $ad-bc\neq0$. Then $ap+bq$ and $cp+dq$ are coprime, and $\max(\deg(ap+bq),\deg(cp+dq))=2$.

{\small\emph{Source:} Standard linear algebra.}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
With $\Delta=ad-bc$, $p=\Delta^{-1}(d(ap+bq)-b(cp+dq))$ and $q=\Delta^{-1}(a(cp+dq)-c(ap+bq))$. A Bézout identity $xp+yq=1$ becomes $\Delta^{-1}(dx-cy)(ap+bq)+\Delta^{-1}(ay-bx)(cp+dq)=1$; and if both new members had degree at most $1$, so would $p$ and $q$.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.qbar_matrix_fin_two_eigen_or_jordan -- https://prove2.me/theorems/412a8540-a8bd-488e-b600-30595d6b20a3
\begin{lemma}[Two-by-two matrices over $\Qbar$]
\label{lem:qbar_matrix_fin_two_eigen_or_jordan}
\lean{Diaz.qbar_matrix_fin_two_eigen_or_jordan}
\leanok
Let $M$ be a $2\times2$ matrix with entries in $\Qbar$, acting on $\Qbar^{2}$. Then $M=cI$ for some $c\in\Qbar$; or there are free $v,w\in\Qbar^{2}$ and $c_1\neq c_2$ in $\Qbar$ with $Mv=c_1v$ and $Mw=c_2w$; or there are free $v,w\in\Qbar^{2}$ and $c\in\Qbar$ with $Mv=cv$ and $Mw=cw+v$.

{\small\emph{Source:} Standard linear algebra: the Jordan form of a $2\times2$ matrix over an algebraically closed field.}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
Explicit, for $M$ with rows $(\alpha,\beta)$ and $(\gamma,\delta)$. If $\beta=0$, the vectors $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$, $(0,\gamma)$ and $(\alpha-\delta,\gamma)$ give the three cases. If $\beta\neq0$, a root $l$ of $t^{2}-(\alpha+\delta)t+\alpha\delta-\beta\gamma$ lies in $\Qbar$, as a square root of the discriminant is algebraic; with the other root $m$, the vectors $(\beta,l-\alpha)$ and $(\beta,m-\alpha)$ are an eigenbasis if $l\neq m$, and $(\beta,l-\alpha)$ and $(0,1)$ a Jordan pair if $l=m$.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.quadratic_ratio_wronskian_free -- https://prove2.me/theorems/ab066b9b-530a-49cb-b006-dcfac08efd4f
\begin{lemma}[The Wronskian quotient is free over $\Qbar(h)$]
\label{lem:quadratic_ratio_wronskian_free}
\lean{Diaz.quadratic_ratio_wronskian_free}
\leanok
Let $u\in\C\setminus\Qbar$. Let $p,q\in\Qbar[X]$ be coprime with $\max(\deg p,\deg q)=2$, $J=p'q-pq'$, $h=p(u)/q(u)$ and $w=J(u)/q(u)$. If $A,B\in\Qbar[X]$ satisfy $A(h)+B(h)w=0$, then $A=B=0$: so $1$ and $w$ are linearly independent over the field $\Qbar(h)$.

{\small\emph{Source:} Not found in the sources read; routine (Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources}).}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
\uses{lem:quadratic_pencil_wronskian_identities,lem:quadratic_pencil_resultant_ne_zero}
$q(u)\neq0$, and $h$ is transcendental, as $p-hq$ would otherwise vanish at $u$. Lemma~\ref{lem:quadratic_pencil_wronskian_identities} at $u$, divided by $q(u)^{2}$, gives $w^{2}=\Delta(h)$ with $\Delta=d_2X^{2}+d_1X+d_0$, so $A^{2}=B^{2}\Delta$ in $\Qbar[X]$. If $B\neq0$, then $B\mid A$ and $\Delta$ is a square, so $d_1^{2}-4d_2d_0=0$; but $d_1^{2}-4d_2d_0=16\Res$, which is non-zero by Lemma~\ref{lem:quadratic_pencil_resultant_ne_zero}.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.quadratic_ratio_pole_fractions_independent -- https://prove2.me/theorems/ba7a6c98-36b5-4799-aec7-d07d9355836d
\begin{lemma}[Pole fractions at three values are free]
\label{lem:quadratic_ratio_pole_fractions_independent}
\lean{Diaz.quadratic_ratio_pole_fractions_independent}
\leanok
Let $u\in\C\setminus\Qbar$. Let $p,q\in\Qbar[X]$ be coprime with $\max(\deg p,\deg q)=2$ and $J=p'q-pq'$. Let $\lambda_0,\lambda_1,\lambda_2\in\Qbar$ be distinct, let $(\alpha_i,\beta_i)\in\Qbar^{2}$ be non-zero for each $i$, and put $g_i=q(u)\bigl(\alpha_iq(u)+\beta_iJ(u)\bigr)/\bigl(u(p(u)-\lambda_iq(u))\bigr)$. Then $1,u,u^{-1},g_0,g_1,g_2$ are free over $\Qbar$: pole fractions at three distinct values of $\lambda$ are free modulo $\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{-1}$.

{\small\emph{Source:} Not found in the sources read; routine (Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources}). Step~1 of the elementary proof of Theorem~NF (Theorem~\ref{thm:degree_two_configuration_normal_form}).}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
\uses{lem:quadratic_pencil_wronskian_span,lem:quadratic_ratio_wronskian_free}
Write $a+bu+cu^{-1}=R(u)/u$ with $R=c+aX+bX^{2}$, and $R=a'q+b'p+c'J$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:quadratic_pencil_wronskian_span}. Dividing a relation by $q(u)/u$ and multiplying it by $\prod_j(h-\lambda_j)$, with $h=p(u)/q(u)$, gives $A(h)+B(h)w=0$ for $w=J(u)/q(u)$, so $A=B=0$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:quadratic_ratio_wronskian_free}; at $X=\lambda_i$ only the $i$-th fraction survives, so $d_i\alpha_i=d_i\beta_i=0$ and $d_i=0$, and then $a=b=c=0$.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.degree_two_configuration_multiplier_complement -- https://prove2.me/theorems/b7f5def8-63f9-4d19-b2c1-1520e8a3748f
\begin{proposition}[A multiplier complement]
\label{prop:degree_two_configuration_multiplier_complement}
\lean{Diaz.degree_two_configuration_multiplier_complement}
\leanok
Let $u\in\C\setminus\Qbar$. Let $W\subseteq\C$ be a $\Qbar$-space of dimension $5$ containing $1$, $u$ and $u^{-1}$. Let $p,q\in\Qbar[X]$ be coprime with $\max(\deg p,\deg q)=2$, and let $y_0,y_1,y_2\in W$ be free over $\Qbar$ with $(p(u)/q(u))y_j\in W$ for every $j$. Then there are $\lambda\in\{0,1,2\}$ and $g_1,g_2\in\C$ such that, with $k=q(u)/(p(u)-\lambda q(u))$, $W=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{-1}+\Qbar g_1+\Qbar g_2$ and $kg_1,kg_2\in W$.

{\small\emph{Source:} Not found in the sources read; routine (Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources}). Steps~1 to~3 of the elementary proof of Theorem~NF (Theorem~\ref{thm:degree_two_configuration_normal_form}).}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
\uses{lem:quadratic_pencil_wronskian_span,lem:quadratic_ratio_pole_fractions_independent}
Step 1: as six free vectors do not fit in $W$, Lemma~\ref{lem:quadratic_ratio_pole_fractions_independent} gives some $\lambda\in\{0,1,2\}$ for which no non-zero pole fraction $g_\lambda(\alpha,\beta)=q(u)(\alpha q(u)+\beta J(u))/(u(p(u)-\lambda q(u)))$ lies in $W$. Step 2: the $Y_j=(p(u)/q(u)-\lambda)y_j$ lie in $W$, are free, and $kY_j=y_j\in W$; for $f\in V\cap(\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{-1})$, $V=\sum_j\Qbar Y_j$, Lemma~\ref{lem:quadratic_pencil_wronskian_span} writes $uf$ as $a'q+b'p+c'J$ at $u$, and $kf-b'q(u)/u=g_\lambda(a'+\lambda b',c')\in W$ forces $f\in\Qbar(p(u)-\lambda q(u))/u$. Step 3: so $\dim(V+\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{-1})\geq5$, $V+\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{-1}=W$, and two of the $Y_j$ serve as $g_1,g_2$.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.quadratic_complement_multiplication_matrix -- https://prove2.me/theorems/7ca6aac2-4dbc-4932-bbea-d64531ea4a5d
\begin{lemma}[Multiplication by $k$ modulo $\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{-1}$]
\label{lem:quadratic_complement_multiplication_matrix}
\lean{Diaz.quadratic_complement_multiplication_matrix}
\leanok
Let $u\in\C\setminus\Qbar$. Let $k,g_0,g_1\in\C$ with $kg_j\in\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{-1}+\Qbar g_0+\Qbar g_1$ for $j=0,1$. Then there are a $2\times2$ matrix $T$ over $\Qbar$ and $R_0,R_1\in\Qbar[X]$ of degree at most $2$ with $kg_j=R_j(u)/u+T_{0j}g_0+T_{1j}g_1$ for $j=0,1$. As the $R(u)/u$ with $\deg R\leq2$ are the elements of $\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{-1}$, $T$ is a matrix of multiplication by $k$ modulo $\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{-1}$; no dimension is assumed, so $T$ need not be unique.

{\small\emph{Source:} Not found in the sources read; routine (Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources}). Part of Step~4 of the elementary proof of Theorem~NF (Theorem~\ref{thm:degree_two_configuration_normal_form}).}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
Write $kg_j=a_j+b_ju+c_ju^{-1}+d_jg_0+e_jg_1$ and take $T_{0j}=d_j$, $T_{1j}=e_j$ and $R_j=b_jX^{2}+a_jX+c_j$; $u\neq0$ as $u\notin\Qbar$.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.quadratic_complement_eigen_forms -- https://prove2.me/theorems/606b4fc0-36c9-4193-bca8-0dcf958516cf
\begin{proposition}[The eigen-forms of the multiplication matrix]
\label{prop:quadratic_complement_eigen_forms}
\lean{Diaz.quadratic_complement_eigen_forms}
\leanok
Let $u\in\C\setminus\Qbar$. Let $P,Q\in\Qbar[X]$ be coprime with $\max(\deg P,\deg Q)=2$, and let $g_0,g_1\in\C$ be such that $S=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{-1}+\Qbar g_0+\Qbar g_1$ has dimension $5$ and $(P(u)/Q(u))g_j\in S$ for $j=0,1$. Write $P_c=P(u)-cQ(u)$. Then one of the following holds:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] the scalar shape: for some $c\in\Qbar$, $Q(u)R(u)/(uP_c)\in S$ for every $R\in\Qbar[X]$ of degree at most $2$;
\item[(ii)] the two-orbit shape: for some $c_1\neq c_2$ in $\Qbar$ and $R_1,R_2\in\Qbar[X]$ of degree at most $2$, $S=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{-1}+\Qbar f_1+\Qbar f_2$ with $f_i=Q(u)R_i(u)/(uP_{c_i})$;
\item[(iii)] the cyclic shape: for some $c\in\Qbar$ and $R_0,R_1\in\Qbar[X]$ of degree at most $2$, $S=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{-1}+\Qbar f_1+\Qbar f_2$ with $f_1=Q(u)R_0(u)/(uP_c)$ and $f_2=Q(u)\bigl(Q(u)R_0(u)+P_cR_1(u)\bigr)/(uP_c^{2})$.
\end{enumerate}

{\small\emph{Source:} Not found in the sources read; routine (Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources}). Step~4 of the elementary proof of Theorem~NF (Theorem~\ref{thm:degree_two_configuration_normal_form}).}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
\uses{lem:qbar_matrix_fin_two_eigen_or_jordan,lem:quadratic_complement_multiplication_matrix}
Lemma~\ref{lem:quadratic_complement_multiplication_matrix} gives $T$ and $R_0,R_1$ for $k=P(u)/Q(u)$; with $G(x)=x_0g_0+x_1g_1$ and $H(x)=x_0R_0+x_1R_1$, $Tx=cx+y$ gives $G(x)=Q(u)\bigl(H(x)(u)+uG(y)\bigr)/(uP_c)$. Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:qbar_matrix_fin_two_eigen_or_jordan} to $T$: an eigenbasis gives the two-orbit shape and a Jordan pair the cyclic one, with the same span; if $T=cI$, multiplication by $k-c=P_c/Q(u)$ maps $g_0,g_1,Q(u)/u$ onto a basis of $\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{-1}$, so $Q(u)R(u)/(uP_c)\in\Qbar g_0+\Qbar g_1+\Qbar Q(u)/u$ for every $R$ of degree at most $2$.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.quadratic_eigen_forms_canonical -- https://prove2.me/theorems/8336089d-5874-43cf-9b29-4c9ec746e31d
\begin{lemma}[The three shapes in canonical form]
\label{lem:quadratic_eigen_forms_canonical}
\lean{Diaz.quadratic_eigen_forms_canonical}
\leanok
Let $u\in\C\setminus\Qbar$. Let $W\subseteq\C$ be a $\Qbar$-space of dimension $5$ containing $1$, $u$ and $u^{-1}$. Let $P,Q\in\Qbar[X]$ be coprime with $\max(\deg P,\deg Q)=2$, write $P_c=P(u)-cQ(u)$, and suppose that $W$ has one of the shapes of Proposition~\ref{prop:quadratic_complement_eigen_forms}, with $W$ for $S$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] the scalar shape: for some $c\in\Qbar$, $Q(u)R(u)/(uP_c)\in W$ for every $R\in\Qbar[X]$ of degree at most $2$;
\item[(ii)] the two-orbit shape: for some $c_1\neq c_2$ in $\Qbar$ and $R_1,R_2\in\Qbar[X]$ of degree at most $2$, $W=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{-1}+\Qbar f_1+\Qbar f_2$ with $f_i=Q(u)R_i(u)/(uP_{c_i})$;
\item[(iii)] the cyclic shape: for some $c\in\Qbar$ and $R_0,R_1\in\Qbar[X]$ of degree at most $2$, $W=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{-1}+\Qbar f_1+\Qbar f_2$ with $f_1=Q(u)R_0(u)/(uP_c)$ and $f_2=Q(u)\bigl(Q(u)R_0(u)+P_cR_1(u)\bigr)/(uP_c^{2})$.
\end{enumerate}
Then $W$ satisfies one of the following:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(D1)] there are $t_0,t_1,t_2\in W$, free over $\Qbar$, with $ut_0,ut_1,ut_2\in W$;
\item[(D2a)] the two-orbit form: for some polynomials $P'$, $Q'$, $S_1$, $S_2$ in $\Qbar[X]$, with $P'$ and $Q'$ coprime, $\max(\deg P',\deg Q')=2$ and $\deg S_1,\deg S_2\leq2$, $W=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{-1}+\Qbar g_1+\Qbar g_2$ with $g_1=Q'(u)S_1(u)/(uP'(u))$ and $g_2=P'(u)S_2(u)/(uQ'(u))$;
\item[(D2b)] the cyclic form: for some such $P',Q',S_1,S_2$, $W=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{-1}+\Qbar g_1+\Qbar g_2$ with $g_1=Q'(u)S_1(u)/(uP'(u))$ and $g_2=Q'(u)\bigl(Q'(u)S_1(u)+P'(u)S_2(u)\bigr)/(uP'(u)^{2})$.
\end{enumerate}

{\small\emph{Source:} Not found in the sources read; routine (Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources}). Step~5 of the elementary proof of Theorem~NF (Theorem~\ref{thm:degree_two_configuration_normal_form}).}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
\uses{lem:coprime_pencil_mobius}
Lemma~\ref{lem:coprime_pencil_mobius} keeps $(P-cQ,Q)$ and, for $c_1\neq c_2$, $(P-c_1Q,P-c_2Q)$ coprime of maximal degree $2$. Scalar: $t=(u^{-1},1,Q(u)/(uP_c))$ and $ut$ lie in $W$ (take $R=1$ and $R=X$), and $t$ is free, as a relation times $uP_c$ is $(a+bX)(P-cQ)+eQ=0$ at the transcendental $u$; this is (D1). Two-orbit: $P'=P-c_1Q$, $Q'=P-c_2Q$, $S_1=R_1/(c_1-c_2)$ and $S_2=-R_2/(c_1-c_2)$ change the two generators by $S_1(u)/u$ and $S_2(u)/u$, which lie in $\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{-1}$; this is (D2a). Cyclic: $P'=P-cQ$, $Q'=Q$, $S_1=R_0$ and $S_2=R_1$ give (D2b).
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.degree_two_configuration_normal_form -- https://prove2.me/theorems/76761d3c-b12b-43ab-8ec3-92176be79f05
\begin{theorem}[Theorem NF: the degree-two normal form]
\label{thm:degree_two_configuration_normal_form}
\lean{Diaz.degree_two_configuration_normal_form}
\leanok
Let $u\in\C\setminus\Qbar$. Let $W\subseteq\C$ be a $\Qbar$-space of dimension $5$ containing $1$, $u$ and $u^{-1}$. Let $x_0,x_1\in\C$ be free over $\Qbar$, and $y_0,y_1,y_2\in\C$ too, with all six products $x_iy_j$ in $W$ (a $2\times3$ configuration in $W$). Let $p,q\in\Qbar[X]$ be coprime with $\max(\deg p,\deg q)=2$, and suppose $x_1q(u)=x_0p(u)$, so that the ratio $x_1/x_0$ is $p(u)/q(u)$. Then $W$ satisfies one of the following:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(D1)] there are $t_0,t_1,t_2\in W$, free over $\Qbar$, with $ut_0,ut_1,ut_2\in W$;
\item[(D2a)] the two-orbit form: for some polynomials $P'$, $Q'$, $S_1$, $S_2$ in $\Qbar[X]$, with $P'$ and $Q'$ coprime, $\max(\deg P',\deg Q')=2$ and $\deg S_1,\deg S_2\leq2$, $W=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{-1}+\Qbar g_1+\Qbar g_2$ with $g_1=Q'(u)S_1(u)/(uP'(u))$ and $g_2=P'(u)S_2(u)/(uQ'(u))$;
\item[(D2b)] the cyclic form: for some such $P',Q',S_1,S_2$, $W=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{-1}+\Qbar g_1+\Qbar g_2$ with $g_1=Q'(u)S_1(u)/(uP'(u))$ and $g_2=Q'(u)\bigl(Q'(u)S_1(u)+P'(u)S_2(u)\bigr)/(uP'(u)^{2})$.
\end{enumerate}
$W$ is not assumed to consist of rational functions of $u$; in cases (D2a) and (D2b) the conclusion shows that it does.

{\small\emph{Source:} \textbf{Not found in the sources read, and not routine} (Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources}). The statement is Theorem~2 of the mission's research notes (round R12), with the normal forms of its Q1.3, which become (D2a) and (D2b) after a change of coordinate, proved there with rank-two vector bundles on $\mathbb P^{1}$; the proof here is elementary. The step from a configuration spanning four dimensions to a progression is \cite[Lemma 4]{BSZ17}. Of the sources on scrolls and on vector bundles on $\mathbb P^{1}$, only the textbook account \cite[Ch.~2]{Rei97} was read; it prints the ingredients of the bundle proof but not the three types (Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources}).}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
\uses{prop:degree_two_configuration_multiplier_complement,lem:coprime_pencil_mobius,prop:quadratic_complement_eigen_forms,lem:quadratic_eigen_forms_canonical}
$x_0\neq0$, and $q(u)\neq0$ by a Bézout identity, so $x_1=hx_0$ with $h=p(u)/q(u)$, and $y'=x_0y$ is free with $y'_j,hy'_j\in W$. Proposition~\ref{prop:degree_two_configuration_multiplier_complement} gives $\lambda\in\{0,1,2\}$ and $W=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{-1}+\Qbar g_1+\Qbar g_2$ with $kg_1,kg_2\in W$, $k=q(u)/(p(u)-\lambda q(u))$; the pencil $P=q$, $Q=p-\lambda q$ is coprime of maximal degree $2$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:coprime_pencil_mobius}, and $k=P(u)/Q(u)$. Proposition~\ref{prop:quadratic_complement_eigen_forms} with $S=W$ gives the scalar, two-orbit or cyclic shape, and Lemma~\ref{lem:quadratic_eigen_forms_canonical} turns it into (D1), (D2a) or (D2b).
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[The two-orbit spaces carry a configuration]
\label{prop:quadratic_two_orbit_space_carries_two_by_three_configuration}
\lean{Diaz.quadratic_two_orbit_space_carries_two_by_three_configuration}
\leanok
Let $u\in\C\setminus\Qbar$. Let $P,Q,R_1,R_2\in\Qbar[X]$ with $\max(\deg P,\deg Q)=2$ and $\deg R_1,\deg R_2\leq2$, and suppose that $W=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{-1}+\Qbar g_1+\Qbar g_2$, with $g_1=Q(u)R_1(u)/(uP(u))$ and $g_2=P(u)R_2(u)/(uQ(u))$, has dimension $5$. {\small\emph{Source:} Not found in the sources read; routine (Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources}). The space is the two-orbit normal form of the mission's research notes (round R12, Q1.3), there in the coordinate $h-c$. \leanok
The five generators are free, so $P(u),Q(u)\neq0$, and $R(u)/u\in\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{-1}$ when $\deg R\leq2$. The products are $Q/u$, $R_2/u$, $g_1$ and $P/u$, $g_2$, $R_1/u$ (values at $u$). $x$ is free, as $a+bP/Q=0$ times $R_2/u$ gives $aR_2/u+bg_2=0$; so is $y$, as a relation has no $g_1$ term and, times $P/Q$, gives $(aP+cR_1)/u+bg_2=0$. Only $u\neq0$ is used.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Five-dimensional spaces of rational functions of $u$]
\label{thm:rational_space_two_by_three_configuration_iff}

\leanok
Let $u\in\C\setminus\Qbar$. Let $W\subseteq\C$ be a $\Qbar$-space of dimension $5$ containing $1$, $u$ and $u^{-1}$. Suppose $W\subseteq\Qbar(u)$. Then $W$ carries a $2\times3$ configuration ($x_0,x_1$ free over $\Qbar$, $y_0,y_1,y_2$ free over $\Qbar$, all six $x_iy_j$ in $W$) if and only if it satisfies one of the following:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(D1)] there are $t_0,t_1,t_2\in W$, free over $\Qbar$, with $ut_0,ut_1,ut_2\in W$;
\item[(D2a)] the two-orbit form: for some polynomials $P'$, $Q'$, $S_1$, $S_2$ in $\Qbar[X]$, with $P'$ and $Q'$ coprime, $\max(\deg P',\deg Q')=2$ and $\deg S_1,\deg S_2\leq2$, $W=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{-1}+\Qbar g_1+\Qbar g_2$ with $g_1=Q'(u)S_1(u)/(uP'(u))$ and $g_2=P'(u)S_2(u)/(uQ'(u))$;
\item[(D2b)] the cyclic form: for some such $P',Q',S_1,S_2$, $W=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{-1}+\Qbar g_1+\Qbar g_2$ with $g_1=Q'(u)S_1(u)/(uP'(u))$ and $g_2=Q'(u)\bigl(Q'(u)S_1(u)+P'(u)S_2(u)\bigr)/(uP'(u)^{2})$.
\end{enumerate}
It is the form of Theorem~F (Theorem~\ref{thm:rational_conj_hull_two_by_three_configuration_iff}) that does not use complex conjugation.

{\small\emph{Source:} \textbf{Not found in the sources read, and not routine} (Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources}): the ``only if'' half, the classification. The configurations of the ``if'' half give, at a candidate, exclusions that are substitutions in Roy's strong six exponentials theorem \cite[Corollary 2]{Roy92}. Applied to the conjugation hulls of rational $z$, with Lemma~\ref{lem:rational_conj_hull_le_adjoin}, it gives the five-dimensional case of Theorem~F (Theorem~\ref{thm:rational_conj_hull_two_by_three_configuration_iff}).}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
\uses{thm:degree_two_configuration_normal_form,prop:quadratic_two_orbit_space_carries_two_by_three_configuration,prop:quadratic_cyclic_space_carries_two_by_three_configuration,lem:rational_space_configuration_coprime_ratio,lem:mobius_ratio_configuration_u_multiplier_triple,lem:two_by_three_configuration_ratio_degree_le_two}
Only if: Lemma~\ref{lem:rational_space_configuration_coprime_ratio} gives the ratio $p(u)/q(u)$ in lowest terms, of degree at most $2$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:two_by_three_configuration_ratio_degree_le_two}; degree $1$ gives (D1) by Lemma~\ref{lem:mobius_ratio_configuration_u_multiplier_triple}, and degree $2$ gives (D1), (D2a) or (D2b) by Theorem~NF (Theorem~\ref{thm:degree_two_configuration_normal_form}). \begin{lemma}[Conjugation hulls of rational functions are rational]
\label{lem:rational_conj_hull_le_adjoin}

Let $u\in\C\setminus\Qbar$. Suppose $u\bar u$ is algebraic, let $z\in\Qbar(u)$, and let $W_z=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar\bar u+\Qbar z+\Qbar\bar z$. Then $u^{-1}\in W_z$ and $W_z\subseteq\Qbar(u)$.

{\small\emph{Source:} Not found in the sources read; routine (Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources}).}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
$\rho=u\bar u$ is algebraic and non-zero, so $u^{-1}=\rho^{-1}\bar u$ and $\bar u=\rho u^{-1}\in\Qbar(u)$. Conjugation maps $\Qbar$ to itself and $u$ into $\Qbar(u)$, so it maps $\Qbar(u)$ into itself, and $\bar z\in\Qbar(u)$. Of $u\notin\Qbar$ only $u\neq0$ is used.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.conj_hull_finrank_four_two_by_three_configuration_iff -- https://prove2.me/theorems/1911bedb-1afb-4db1-be0b-a943e00c12ef
\begin{proposition}[Four-dimensional conjugation hulls]
\label{prop:conj_hull_finrank_four_two_by_three_configuration_iff}
\lean{Diaz.conj_hull_finrank_four_two_by_three_configuration_iff}
\leanok
Let $u\in\C\setminus\Qbar$. Suppose $u\bar u$ is algebraic, let $z\in\C$, and suppose that $W_z=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar\bar u+\Qbar z+\Qbar\bar z$ has dimension $4$. Then $W_z$ carries a $2\times3$ configuration ($x_0,x_1$ free over $\Qbar$, $y_0,y_1,y_2$ free over $\Qbar$, all six $x_iy_j$ in $W_z$) if and only if $z\in\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar\bar u+\Qbar(u-a)^{-1}$ for some $a\in\Qbar$ with $a\bar a=u\bar u$. Then $W_z=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar\bar u+\Qbar(u-a)^{-1}$, with $a$ on the circle $|a|=|u|$.

{\small\emph{Source:} Not found in the sources read; routine (Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources}), given Theorem~B (Theorem~\ref{thm:circle_point_extension_two_by_three_configuration_iff}) and the conjugation stability of the hull. The configuration is printed: rescaled, it is \cite[Théorème 7(1)]{Dia07} at $v=1/(u-a)$, and at a candidate the exclusion of $1/(u-a)$ is \cite[Corollaire 5(4)]{Dia07}.}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
\uses{thm:circle_point_extension_two_by_three_configuration_iff}
Put $H_0=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar\bar u$, of dimension $3$. As $\dim W_z=4$, $z\notin H_0$ and $\bar z\in H_0+\Qbar z$, so $W_z=H_0+\Qbar z$ and Theorem~B (Theorem~\ref{thm:circle_point_extension_two_by_three_configuration_iff}) applies. If: $a\bar a=u\bar u\neq0$ gives $a\neq0$, and Theorem~B's third alternative. Only if: Theorem~B gives $W_z=H_0+\Qbar w$ with $w=u^{2}$, $\bar u^{2}$ or $(u-a)^{-1}$, $a\neq0$, and $\bar w\in W_z$. For $w=u^{2}$ or $\bar u^{2}$ this makes $u$ algebraic; for $w=(u-a)^{-1}$ it puts $(u-b)^{-1}$, $b=u\bar u/\bar a$, in $H_0+\Qbar w$, and clearing denominators and evaluating at $b$ gives $b=a$, that is $a\bar a=u\bar u$.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.rational_conj_hull_two_by_three_configuration_iff -- https://prove2.me/theorems/85705356-aa3c-438b-8ce2-9ed394d5e8fb
\begin{theorem}[Theorem F: conjugation hulls of rational functions of $u$]
\label{thm:rational_conj_hull_two_by_three_configuration_iff}
\lean{Diaz.rational_conj_hull_two_by_three_configuration_iff}
\leanok
Let $u\in\C\setminus\Qbar$. Suppose $u\bar u$ is algebraic, let $z\in\Qbar(u)$, and let $W_z=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar\bar u+\Qbar z+\Qbar\bar z$ be its conjugation hull. Then $W_z$ carries a $2\times3$ configuration ($x_0,x_1$ free over $\Qbar$, $y_0,y_1,y_2$ free over $\Qbar$, all six $x_iy_j$ in $W_z$) if and only if $\dim W_z=4$ and $z\in\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar\bar u+\Qbar(u-a)^{-1}$ for some $a\in\Qbar$ with $a\bar a=u\bar u$, or $\dim W_z=5$ and $W_z$ satisfies one of the following:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(D1)] there are $t_0,t_1,t_2\in W_z$, free over $\Qbar$, with $ut_0,ut_1,ut_2\in W_z$;
\item[(D2a)] the two-orbit form: for some polynomials $P'$, $Q'$, $S_1$, $S_2$ in $\Qbar[X]$, with $P'$ and $Q'$ coprime, $\max(\deg P',\deg Q')=2$ and $\deg S_1,\deg S_2\leq2$, $W_z=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{-1}+\Qbar g_1+\Qbar g_2$ with $g_1=Q'(u)S_1(u)/(uP'(u))$ and $g_2=P'(u)S_2(u)/(uQ'(u))$;
\item[(D2b)] the cyclic form: for some such $P',Q',S_1,S_2$, $W_z=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{-1}+\Qbar g_1+\Qbar g_2$ with $g_1=Q'(u)S_1(u)/(uP'(u))$ and $g_2=Q'(u)\bigl(Q'(u)S_1(u)+P'(u)S_2(u)\bigr)/(uP'(u)^{2})$.
\end{enumerate}
Since $\bar u=(u\bar u)u^{-1}$, the polynomials $z$ in $u$ and $\bar u$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:laurent_conj_hull_two_by_three_configuration_iff} (Theorem~E) are among these.

{\small\emph{Source:} \textbf{Not found in the sources read, and not routine} (Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources}): the ``only if'' half, the classification. Theorem~F asks the question of Theorem~E (Theorem~\ref{thm:laurent_conj_hull_two_by_three_configuration_iff}) for every $z$ rational in $u$, and builds on Theorem~B (Theorem~\ref{thm:circle_point_extension_two_by_three_configuration_iff}), which holds for every complex $z$. For $z$ a polynomial in $u$ and $\bar u$ with a five-dimensional hull, its answer gives back the classes (P), (Q) and (R) of Theorem~E (Corollary~\ref{cor:laurent_conj_hull_configuration_shape_iff_class}, with the explicit maps of Lemmas~\ref{lem:laurent_polynomial_class_conj_hull_two_orbit_form}, \ref{lem:laurent_involution_class_space_cyclic_form} and~\ref{lem:laurent_real_pencil_class_space_u_multiplier_triple}); as that proof goes through Theorem~E, the explicit criteria of Corollaries~\ref{cor:laurent_conj_hull_large_exponent_configuration_iff_real_pencil_class} and~\ref{cor:cubic_window_conj_hull_two_by_three_configuration_iff_criterion} still do not follow from Theorem~F. Special cases of the ``if'' half are printed: in dimension $4$ the configuration is \cite[Théorème 7(1)]{Dia07} at $v=1/(u-a)$, with the exclusion at a candidate in \cite[Corollaire 5(4)]{Dia07}; for polynomials of degree $2$ and $3$ in $u$ it is \cite[Théorème 7(1)]{Dia07}; class (Q) of Theorem~E is a substitution in \cite[Théorème 2]{Dia04} and \cite[Théorème 4(1)]{Dia07}. At a candidate, its configurations give exclusions that are substitutions in Roy's strong six exponentials theorem \cite[Corollary 2]{Roy92}; Corollary~\ref{cor:candidate_rational_conj_hull_criterion_not_mem_logAlgTilde} states them.}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
\uses{thm:rational_space_two_by_three_configuration_iff,lem:rational_conj_hull_le_adjoin,prop:conj_hull_finrank_four_two_by_three_configuration_iff,cor:circle_point_config_card_le_four}
$\dim W_z\in\{3,4,5\}$, as $\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar\bar u$ has dimension $3$. In dimension $3$ there is no configuration, by Corollary~\ref{cor:circle_point_config_card_le_four} ($2+3>4$); dimension $4$ is Proposition~\ref{prop:conj_hull_finrank_four_two_by_three_configuration_iff}; in dimension $5$, Lemma~\ref{lem:rational_conj_hull_le_adjoin} puts $u^{-1}$ in $W_z\subseteq\Qbar(u)$, and Theorem~\ref{thm:rational_space_two_by_three_configuration_iff} applies to $W=W_z$.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.degree_one_multiplier_space_visible_or_degree_one_space -- https://prove2.me/theorems/a3ae9ca7-9f2c-4dc3-9cce-e72ef3936e06
\begin{proposition}[Three $u$-multipliers]
\label{prop:degree_one_multiplier_space_visible_or_degree_one_space}
\lean{Diaz.degree_one_multiplier_space_visible_or_degree_one_space}
\leanok
Let $u\in\C\setminus\Qbar$. Let $W\subseteq\C$ be a $\Qbar$-space of dimension $5$ containing $1$, $u$ and $u^{-1}$. Then there are $t_0,t_1,t_2\in W$, free over $\Qbar$, with $ut_0,ut_1,ut_2\in W$ (condition (D1)) if and only if $u^{2}\in W$, or $u^{-2}\in W$, or $(u-a)^{-1}\in W$ for some $a\in\Qbar$ with $a\neq0$, or $W=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{-1}+\Qbar g+\Qbar ug$ for some $g\in\C$ with $1,u,u^{-1},g,ug$ free. The alternatives before the last say that $W$ is visible: it contains $u^{2}$, $u^{-2}$ or $(u-a)^{-1}$, the elements of Theorem~B (when $u\bar u$ is algebraic, $u^{-2}$ is an algebraic multiple of $\bar u^{2}$); the last is a degree-one space.

{\small\emph{Source:} Not found in the sources read; routine (Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources}).}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
If every $t_j$ lies in $\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{-1}$, which has dimension $3$, then $u\in\sum_j\Qbar t_j$ and $u^{2}\in W$. Otherwise take $g=t_j\notin\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{-1}$: if $(u-c)g\in\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{-1}$ for some $c\in\Qbar$, then $u^{-2}\in W$ (for $c=0$) or $(u-c)^{-1}\in W$ (for $c\neq0$); if not, $1,u,u^{-1},g,ug$ are free and span $W$. Conversely take $t=(1,u,u^{-1})$, $(1,u^{-1},u^{-2})$, $(1,u^{-1},(u-a)^{-1})$, as $u(u-a)^{-1}=1+a(u-a)^{-1}$, or $(1,u^{-1},g)$.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.conj_stable_degree_one_multiplier_space_visible_or_real_pencil_space -- https://prove2.me/theorems/bd7526f9-422a-408b-aacb-ac5532fe7917
\begin{proposition}[Conjugation-stable spaces with three $u$-multipliers]
\label{prop:conj_stable_degree_one_multiplier_space_visible_or_real_pencil_space}
\lean{Diaz.conj_stable_degree_one_multiplier_space_visible_or_real_pencil_space}
\leanok
Let $u\in\C\setminus\Qbar$. Let $s\in\Qbar$ be real with $s^{2}=u\bar u$. Let $W\subseteq\C$ be a $\Qbar$-space of dimension $5$ containing $1$, $u$ and $u^{-1}$. Suppose $W$ is stable under complex conjugation and satisfies (D1): there are $t_0,t_1,t_2\in W$, free over $\Qbar$, with $ut_0,ut_1,ut_2\in W$. Then $W$ contains $u^{2}$, $\bar u^{2}$ or some $(u-a)^{-1}$ with $a\in\Qbar$, $a\neq0$, or $W=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar\bar u+\Qbar f+\Qbar f/(s+\lambda u)$ for some $\lambda\in\Qbar$ with $\lambda\bar\lambda=1$ and some real $f\in\C$: a real pencil space $W(\lambda,f)$ of Proposition~\ref{prop:conj_stable_real_pencil_space_carries_two_by_three_configuration}.

{\small\emph{Source:} Not found in the sources read; routine (Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources}), given Theorem~\ref{thm:conj_equivariant_degree_one_space_eq_real_pencil_space}. It is the conjugation-stable refinement of the degree-one case in the mission's research notes (round R10).}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
\uses{prop:degree_one_multiplier_space_visible_or_degree_one_space,thm:conj_equivariant_degree_one_space_eq_real_pencil_space}
As $\bar u=s^{2}u^{-1}$, $u^{-2}\in W$ if and only if $\bar u^{2}\in W$. If $W$ is not visible, Proposition~\ref{prop:degree_one_multiplier_space_visible_or_degree_one_space} gives $W=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{-1}+\Qbar g+\Qbar ug$ with these five free. Then $Z=\{h\in W:uh\in W\}$ is $\Qbar+\Qbar u^{-1}+\Qbar g$, since an eigenvector of $u$ on $W/(\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{-1})$, whose eigenvalue is a root of a quadratic over $\Qbar$, would put $u^{-2}$ or some $(u-c)^{-1}$ in $W$; and $u^{-1}\bar g=s^{-2}\,\overline{ug}$ lies in $Z$, so $\bar g\in\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar ug$. Then $1,u,\bar u,g,ug$ are free and span $W$, and Theorem~\ref{thm:conj_equivariant_degree_one_space_eq_real_pencil_space} gives $\lambda$ and $f$.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.laurent_polynomial_class_conj_hull_two_orbit_form -- https://prove2.me/theorems/aa05d508-a30f-4f4c-9fe6-893fbb763388
\begin{lemma}[Class (P) is a two-orbit space]
\label{lem:laurent_polynomial_class_conj_hull_two_orbit_form}
\lean{Diaz.laurent_polynomial_class_conj_hull_two_orbit_form}
\leanok
Let $u\in\C\setminus\Qbar$. Let $s\in\Qbar$ with $s^{2}=u\bar u$, and put $v=u/s$. Let $k\geq0$, let $c_j\in\C$ for $j\in\Z$ be arbitrary, and put $z=\sum_{j=-k}^{k}c_jv^{j}$ and $W=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar\bar u+\Qbar z+\Qbar\bar z$. Let $\alpha,\beta\in\Qbar$, not both zero, with $\alpha u^{2}+\beta u^{3}\in W$ (class (P) of Theorem~E, Theorem~\ref{thm:laurent_conj_hull_two_by_three_configuration_iff}). Then there are $P',Q',S_1,S_2\in\Qbar[X]$ with $P'(u)=u^{2}$, $Q'(u)=1$, $S_1(u)=\bar\beta s^{6}+\bar\alpha s^{4}u$ and $S_2(u)=\alpha u+\beta u^{2}$, such that $P',Q'$ are coprime, $\max(\deg P',\deg Q')=2$, $\deg S_1,\deg S_2\leq2$, and $W=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{-1}+\Qbar g_1+\Qbar g_2$ with $g_1=Q'(u)S_1(u)/(uP'(u))$ and $g_2=P'(u)S_2(u)/(uQ'(u))$. So $W$ has the two-orbit shape (D2a) of Theorem~F (Theorem~\ref{thm:rational_conj_hull_two_by_three_configuration_iff}) for the pencil $(X^{2},1)$, and $W=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{-1}+\Qbar\bar w+\Qbar w$ for $w=\alpha u^{2}+\beta u^{3}$. No dimension is assumed, and the $c_j$ need not be algebraic.

{\small\emph{Source:} Not found in the sources read; routine (Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources}). It writes class (P) of Theorem~E in the coordinates of Theorem~F (Theorem~\ref{thm:rational_conj_hull_two_by_three_configuration_iff}). The configuration of class (P) is printed: \cite[Théorème 7(1)]{Dia07}, already in \cite[Théorème 2]{Dia04}.}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
As $u\neq0$ and $s^{2}=u\bar u$, $s\neq0$ and $\bar u=s^{2}/u$, so $\bar w=(\bar\beta s^{6}+\bar\alpha s^{4}u)/u^{3}$; with $P'=X^{2}$, $Q'=1$, $S_1=\bar\beta s^{6}+\bar\alpha s^{4}X$ and $S_2=\alpha X+\beta X^{2}$, whose coefficients are algebraic, the two generators are $g_1=\bar w$ and $g_2=w$. The five numbers $1,u,u^{-1},\bar w,w$ lie in $W$: $u^{-1}=s^{-2}\bar u$, and $W$ is stable under conjugation, which permutes its generators. They are free: a relation times $u^{3}$ is a polynomial of degree at most $6$ in the transcendental $u$, with coefficients $x_3\bar\beta s^{6},x_3\bar\alpha s^{4},x_2,x_0,x_1,x_4\alpha,x_4\beta$. As $W$ is spanned by five numbers, the inclusion is an equality.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.laurent_involution_class_space_cyclic_form -- https://prove2.me/theorems/00e48e2c-49f1-4fe9-822b-495d0b8e830a
\begin{lemma}[Class (Q) is a cyclic space]
\label{lem:laurent_involution_class_space_cyclic_form}
\lean{Diaz.laurent_involution_class_space_cyclic_form}
\leanok
Let $u\in\C\setminus\Qbar$. Let $s\in\Qbar$ with $s^{2}=u\bar u$, and put $v=u/s$. Let $e,\beta,\zeta\in\Qbar$ with $\beta\neq0$. Then there are $P',Q',S_1,S_2\in\Qbar[X]$ with $P'(u)=su$, $Q'(u)=u^{2}+\beta s^{2}$, $S_1(u)=s/\beta+(e/s)u^{2}$ and $S_2(u)=(\zeta/s)u^{2}$, such that $P',Q'$ are coprime, $\max(\deg P',\deg Q')=2$, $\deg S_1,\deg S_2\leq2$, and
\[\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar\bar u+\Qbar(\bar v^{2}+ev^{2})+\Qbar(\beta\bar v^{3}+\zeta v^{2}+ev^{3})=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{-1}+\Qbar g_1+\Qbar g_2\]
with $g_1=Q'(u)S_1(u)/(uP'(u))$ and $g_2=Q'(u)\bigl(Q'(u)S_1(u)+P'(u)S_2(u)\bigr)/(uP'(u)^{2})$. The left side is the space of class (Q) of Theorem~E (Theorem~\ref{thm:laurent_conj_hull_two_by_three_configuration_iff}), which asks in addition $e\bar e=\beta\bar\beta=1$ and $\zeta=-\beta e^{2}\bar\zeta$; the identity needs none of these, and no dimension. So every hull of class (Q) has the cyclic shape (D2b) of Theorem~F (Theorem~\ref{thm:rational_conj_hull_two_by_three_configuration_iff}) for the pencil $(sX,X^{2}+\beta s^{2})$.

{\small\emph{Source:} Not found in the sources read; routine (Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources}). An identity of spans that writes class (Q) of Theorem~E in the coordinates of Theorem~F. The ratio $Q'(u)/P'(u)=(u+\beta\bar u)/s$ of the pencil is that of the configuration of class (Q), which is printed: the proof of \cite[Théorème 2]{Dia04}, at $x=(1,(u+\beta\bar u)/s)$; also \cite[Théorème 4(1)]{Dia07}.}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
$s$ is real and non-zero, as $s^{2}=|u|^{2}>0$, so $\bar u=s^{2}/u$ and $\bar v=s/u$. The pencil is coprime by the Bézout identity $-(\beta s^{3})^{-1}X\cdot P'+(\beta s^{2})^{-1}Q'=1$. With $n_0=\bar v^{2}+ev^{2}$ and $n_1=\beta\bar v^{3}+\zeta v^{2}+ev^{3}$, two exact identities hold: $g_1-n_0=\beta e+\beta^{-1}$ and $g_2-n_1=\beta\zeta+((2\beta e+\beta^{-1})/s)u+((\beta^{2}e+2)/s)\bar u$. Both differences lie in $\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar\bar u=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{-1}$, so each generator of either side is an explicit combination of those of the other.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.laurent_real_pencil_class_space_u_multiplier_triple -- https://prove2.me/theorems/bf190dc0-3812-4920-8dcc-4e8e2e6fa6a6
\begin{lemma}[Class (R) has three $u$-multipliers]
\label{lem:laurent_real_pencil_class_space_u_multiplier_triple}
\lean{Diaz.laurent_real_pencil_class_space_u_multiplier_triple}
\leanok
Let $u\in\C\setminus\Qbar$. Let $s\in\Qbar$ with $s^{2}=u\bar u$, and put $v=u/s$. Let $\kappa\in\Qbar$ with $\kappa\bar\kappa=1$ and $G\in\Qbar[X]$ with $\deg G\geq1$, and put $g=G(v)+\kappa\,\overline{vG(v)}$ and $W=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar\bar u+\Qbar g+\Qbar\bar g$. Then $u^{-1},1,g$ are free over $\Qbar$, and $t=(u^{-1},1,g)$ has $t_j\in W$ and $ut_j\in W$ for $j=0,1,2$. So $W$ has the shape (D1) of Theorem~F (Theorem~\ref{thm:rational_conj_hull_two_by_three_configuration_iff}); class (R) of Theorem~E (Theorem~\ref{thm:laurent_conj_hull_two_by_three_configuration_iff}) asks in addition $G(0)=0$ and $\deg G\geq2$, so every hull of class (R) has shape (D1).

{\small\emph{Source:} Not found in the sources read; routine (Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources}). A change of coordinates in Lemma~\ref{lem:laurent_real_pencil_normal_form_carries_two_by_three_configuration}, which gives the configuration of class (R) with the triple $(\bar v,1,g)$. The real pencil spaces are the project's (Proposition~\ref{prop:conj_stable_real_pencil_space_carries_two_by_three_configuration}).}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
\uses{lem:laurent_real_pencil_normal_form_carries_two_by_three_configuration}
$s$ is real and non-zero, so $v\bar v=1$, $v\notin\Qbar$ and $u^{-1}=s^{-1}\bar v$. Lemma~\ref{lem:laurent_real_pencil_normal_form_carries_two_by_three_configuration} makes $\bar v,1,g$ free, and rescaling $\bar v$ by $s^{-1}\in\Qbar$ keeps them free. The numbers $u^{-1}=s^{-2}\bar u$, $1$ and $g$ lie in $W$; $u\cdot u^{-1}=1$ and $u\cdot1=u$; and $vg=vG(v)+\kappa v\bar v\,\overline{G(v)}=\kappa\bar g$, as $v\bar v=\kappa\bar\kappa=1$, so $ug=s\kappa\bar g\in W$.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.laurent_conj_hull_configuration_shape_iff_class -- https://prove2.me/theorems/0e35095f-1635-43b5-b8be-fb64c275ee02
\begin{corollary}[The shapes of Theorem F and the classes of Theorem E agree]
\label{cor:laurent_conj_hull_configuration_shape_iff_class}
\lean{Diaz.laurent_conj_hull_configuration_shape_iff_class}
\leanok
Let $u\in\C\setminus\Qbar$. Let $s\in\Qbar$ with $s^{2}=u\bar u$, and put $v=u/s$. Let $k\geq0$, let $c_j\in\Qbar$ for $j\in\Z$, and put $z=\sum_{j=-k}^{k}c_jv^{j}$ and $W=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar\bar u+\Qbar z+\Qbar\bar z$. Suppose $\dim W=5$. Then $W$ has one of the shapes of Theorem~F (Theorem~\ref{thm:rational_conj_hull_two_by_three_configuration_iff}),
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(D1)] there are $t_0,t_1,t_2\in W$, free over $\Qbar$, with $ut_0,ut_1,ut_2\in W$;
\item[(D2a)] the two-orbit form: for some polynomials $P'$, $Q'$, $S_1$, $S_2$ in $\Qbar[X]$, with $P'$ and $Q'$ coprime, $\max(\deg P',\deg Q')=2$ and $\deg S_1,\deg S_2\leq2$, $W=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{-1}+\Qbar g_1+\Qbar g_2$ with $g_1=Q'(u)S_1(u)/(uP'(u))$ and $g_2=P'(u)S_2(u)/(uQ'(u))$;
\item[(D2b)] the cyclic form: for some such $P',Q',S_1,S_2$, $W=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{-1}+\Qbar g_1+\Qbar g_2$ with $g_1=Q'(u)S_1(u)/(uP'(u))$ and $g_2=Q'(u)\bigl(Q'(u)S_1(u)+P'(u)S_2(u)\bigr)/(uP'(u)^{2})$.
\end{enumerate}
if and only if it is in one of the classes of Theorem~E (Theorem~\ref{thm:laurent_conj_hull_two_by_three_configuration_iff}),
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(P)] $\alpha u^{2}+\beta u^{3}\in W$ for some $\alpha,\beta\in\Qbar$, not both zero;
\item[(Q)] $W=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar\bar u+\Qbar(\bar v^{2}+ev^{2})+\Qbar(\beta\bar v^{3}+\zeta v^{2}+ev^{3})$ for some $e,\beta,\zeta\in\Qbar$ with $e\bar e=\beta\bar\beta=1$ and $\zeta=-\beta e^{2}\bar\zeta$;
\item[(R)] $W=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar\bar u+\Qbar g+\Qbar\bar g$ with $g=G(v)+\kappa\,\overline{vG(v)}$, for some $\kappa\in\Qbar$ with $\kappa\bar\kappa=1$ and some $G\in\Qbar[X]$ with $G(0)=0$ and $\deg G\geq2$.
\end{enumerate}
Both theorems say when $W$ carries a $2\times3$ configuration; for Laurent $z$ their criteria agree. The explicit maps are Lemmas~\ref{lem:laurent_polynomial_class_conj_hull_two_orbit_form}, \ref{lem:laurent_involution_class_space_cyclic_form} and~\ref{lem:laurent_real_pencil_class_space_u_multiplier_triple}: (P) to (D2a), (Q) to (D2b), and (R) to (D1).

{\small\emph{Source:} Not found in the sources read; routine (Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources}). \begin{proposition}[The multiplier space of a degree-two configuration]
\label{prop:degree_two_configuration_multiplier_space_eq}
\lean{Diaz.degree_two_configuration_multiplier_space_eq}
\leanok
Let $u\in\C\setminus\Qbar$. Let $W\subseteq\C$ be a $\Qbar$-space of dimension $5$ containing $1$, $u$ and $u^{-1}$. Let $x_0,x_1\in\C$ be free over $\Qbar$, and $y_0,y_1,y_2\in\C$ too, with all six products $x_iy_j$ in $W$. Let $p,q\in\Qbar[X]$ be coprime with $\max(\deg p,\deg q)=2$, and suppose $x_1q(u)=x_0p(u)$, so that the ratio $x_1/x_0$ is $h=p(u)/q(u)$. Then, for every $f\in\C$, $f\in W$ and $hf\in W$ if and only if $f\in\Qbar x_0y_0+\Qbar x_0y_1+\Qbar x_0y_2$; and $W\cap h^{-1}W=\{f\in W:hf\in W\}$ has dimension $3$. This is the setting of Theorem~NF (Theorem~\ref{thm:degree_two_configuration_normal_form}), and the conclusion is the uniqueness of the configuration with ratio $h$: the span of the products $x_0y_j$ is $W\cap h^{-1}W$, which depends only on $W$ and $h$.

{\small\emph{Source:} Not found in the sources read; routine (Chapter~\ref{chap:14-not-found-in-the-sources}). It adds what the formal statement of Theorem~NF (Theorem~\ref{thm:degree_two_configuration_normal_form}) leaves out, the uniqueness part of the normal form of the mission's research notes (round R12): the span of the products depends only on $W$ and $h$. The proof is that of Proposition~\ref{prop:degree_two_configuration_multiplier_complement}, run on all of $W\cap k_0^{-1}W$.}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
\leanok
\uses{lem:quadratic_pencil_wronskian_span,lem:quadratic_ratio_pole_fractions_independent}
$q(u)\neq0$, so $h=x_1/x_0$. The $y'_j=x_0y_j$ are free, lie in $W$ and have $hy'_j=x_1y_j\in W$, so they lie in $Z=\{f\in W:hf\in W\}$. As in Proposition~\ref{prop:degree_two_configuration_multiplier_complement}, Lemma~\ref{lem:quadratic_ratio_pole_fractions_independent} gives $\lambda\in\{0,1,2\}$ for which no non-zero pole fraction $g_\lambda(\alpha,\beta)=q(u)(\alpha q(u)+\beta J(u))/(u(p(u)-\lambda q(u)))$, $J=p'q-pq'$, lies in $W$. Put $E=p(u)-\lambda q(u)$, $k_0=q(u)/E$ and $N'=\{g\in W:k_0g\in W\}$. If $f\in\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{-1}$ and $k_0f\in W$, Lemma~\ref{lem:quadratic_pencil_wronskian_span} writes $uf=a'q(u)+b'p(u)+c'J(u)$, and $k_0f-b'q(u)/u=g_\lambda(a'+\lambda b',c')\in W$ forces $f=b'E/u$; so $N'$ meets $\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{-1}$ in at most a line, and $\dim N'\leq5+1-3=3$. The space $V=(h-\lambda)(\Qbar y'_0+\Qbar y'_1+\Qbar y'_2)$ has dimension $3$ and lies in $N'$, so $V=N'$. For $f\in Z$, $(h-\lambda)f\in N'=V$, and cancelling $h-\lambda\neq0$ gives $f\in\Qbar y'_0+\Qbar y'_1+\Qbar y'_2$.
\end{proof}

% Prove2Me: DiazModulus.candidate_rational_conj_hull_criterion_not_mem_logAlgTilde -- https://prove2.me/theorems/33dd25ff-3644-4181-b5b2-9c9796bc19be
\begin{corollary}[The criterion of Theorem F at a candidate]
\label{cor:candidate_rational_conj_hull_criterion_not_mem_logAlgTilde}
\lean{Diaz.candidate_rational_conj_hull_criterion_not_mem_logAlgTilde}
\leanok
Assume Roy's strong six exponentials theorem: there is no $2\times3$ configuration in $\widetilde{\mathcal L}$, the $\Qbar$-span of $1$ and the logarithms of algebraic numbers. Let $u$ be a candidate: $u\neq0$, $|u|$ algebraic and $e^{u}$ algebraic. Let $z\in\Qbar(u)$, the field generated by $\Qbar$ and $u$, and let $W_z=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar\bar u+\Qbar z+\Qbar\bar z$ be its conjugation hull. Suppose $W_z$ meets the criterion of Theorem~F (Theorem~\ref{thm:rational_conj_hull_two_by_three_configuration_iff}): $\dim W_z=4$ and $z\in\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar\bar u+\Qbar(u-a)^{-1}$ for some $a\in\Qbar$ with $a\bar a=u\bar u$, or $\dim W_z=5$ and $W_z$ satisfies one of the following:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(D1)] there are $t_0,t_1,t_2\in W_z$, free over $\Qbar$, with $ut_0,ut_1,ut_2\in W_z$;
\item[(D2a)] the two-orbit form: for some polynomials $P'$, $Q'$, $S_1$, $S_2$ in $\Qbar[X]$, with $P'$ and $Q'$ coprime, $\max(\deg P',\deg Q')=2$ and $\deg S_1,\deg S_2\leq2$, $W_z=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{-1}+\Qbar g_1+\Qbar g_2$ with $g_1=Q'(u)S_1(u)/(uP'(u))$ and $g_2=P'(u)S_2(u)/(uQ'(u))$;
\item[(D2b)] the cyclic form: for some such $P',Q',S_1,S_2$, $W_z=\Qbar+\Qbar u+\Qbar u^{-1}+\Qbar g_1+\Qbar g_2$ with $g_1=Q'(u)S_1(u)/(uP'(u))$ and $g_2=Q'(u)\bigl(Q'(u)S_1(u)+P'(u)S_2(u)\bigr)/(uP'(u)^{2})$.
\end{enumerate}
Then $z\notin\widetilde{\mathcal L}$.

\begin{proof}
\leanok
\uses{thm:rational_conj_hull_two_by_three_configuration_iff,thm:hermite_lindemann_holds,lem:logAlg_conj_stable,lem:logAlgTilde_conj_stable}
Theorem~\ref{thm:hermite_lindemann_holds} gives $u\notin\Qbar$, as $u\neq0$ and $e^{u}$ is algebraic, and $u\bar u=|u|^{2}$ is algebraic. So Theorem~F applies to $z$, and its ``if'' half puts a configuration in $W_z$. If $z\in\widetilde{\mathcal L}$, then $W_z\subseteq\widetilde{\mathcal L}$: $u\in\mathcal L$, $\bar u\in\mathcal L$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:logAlg_conj_stable}) and $\bar z\in\widetilde{\mathcal L}$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:logAlgTilde_conj_stable}); the configuration then lies in $\widetilde{\mathcal L}$, against Roy's theorem.
\end{proof}
